questionStem: A 20-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 0, at 36 weeks' gestation delivers a stillborn infant. She had no prenatal care, and the prenatal course was complicated by maternal cocaine and alcohol use. She also was seen in the emergency department at 20 weeks' gestation after being assaulted by her boyfriend . Examination at the time showed scalp and forearm lacerations and bruising of the abdomen and face . She took phenytoin during the pregnancy for a seizure disorder ; she had no seizures during the pregnancy . An autopsy of the fetus shows multiple fractures of thin ribs and multiple fractures of the rather broad and ribbon-shaped tubular bones. Examination of the fetus shows blue sclerae , soft calvaria , a small chest, and bent short extremities . Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?

choices.C: Intrauterine trauma resulting from abuse to the mothe

correctExplanation: This infant likely died from complications of osteogenesis imperfecta, which results from mutations or posttranslational defects in collagen, type I. Given the presence of collagen, type I, in bone, skin, and connective tissues, pathology results from connective tissue defects ranging in severity from postpubertal fractures to fatal fractures in utero. The presentation of this fetus likely reflects fragile long bones along with decreased calvarial ossification and thin sclerae (leading to visualization of the choroidal veins). Patients may also present with short stature, scoliosis, basilar skull deformities (leading to nerve compression), hearing loss (likely related to abnormal bone formation in the ossicles and cochlea), opalescent and fragile teeth, and easy bruising (caused by collagen, type I, defects in blood vessel walls). Treatment is primarily supportive, involving possible bisphosphonates along with monitoring for complications, physical therapy, and genetic counseling.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alcohol-induced fetal abnormalities (Choice B) include intellectual disability, developmental delay, and physical malformations such as microcephaly, facial dysmorphia, limb deformities, and congenital heart disease. Patients with fetal alcohol syndrome may demonstrate abnormal bone development (eg, cervical spine fusion) and delayed bone growth. However, osseous fragility would be atypical. Intrauterine trauma resulting from abuse to the mother (Choice C) may lead to increased fetal cortisol production and stress physiology. However, in the absence of a blunt or penetrating injury to the mother, mechanical trauma to the fetus would be unlikely. Placental insufficiency from cocaine use (Choice D) can lead to preterm birth, intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight, and placental abruption. However, osseous fragility would be atypical. Teratogenicity of phenytoin (Choice E) commonly causes orofacial clefts, cardiac malformations, and genitourinary defects. In adults, phenytoin may cause osteomalacia as a result of changes in calcium metabolism. However, maternal phenytoin use is unlikely to result in osseous fragility in infants. Educational Objective: In osteogenesis imperfecta, abnormalities of collagen, type I, lead to connective tissue defects and consequent bone fractures, scoliosis, short stature, skull deformities, blue sclera, fragile teeth, hearing loss, and easy bruising. Severe cases lead to death in utero.

questionStem: A previously healthy 1-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of increasing weakness and difficulty feeding . He is alert. Examination shows tongue fasciculations and profound hypotonia . Deep tendon reflexes are absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient most likely has progressive infantile spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). SMA commonly involves an autosomal recessive mutation of the SMN protein, resulting in defective mRNA synthesis in motor neurons. The infantile form of SMA typically affects normally developing infants who are several months old. In spinal muscular atrophy, the bilateral lower brainstem motor nuclei and anterior horns degenerate, leading to progressive, symmetric muscular weakness and a lower motor neuron-pattern of dysfunction (eg, decreased tone, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, early-onset atrophy). The lower extremities are typically more affected than the upper extremities. Dysfunction progresses over the course of months. In severe cases, progressive respiratory insufficiency may develop. The diagnosis can be confirmed with genetic testing. Treatment is supportive and includes promoting nutrition, motor, and respiratory function.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Botulism (Choice A) is an acute disease of the neuromuscular junction caused by the exposure to the C/ostridium botulinum toxin (eg, in raw honey). Over the course of hours to days, patients develop symmetric hypotonia and hyporeflexia that begins with the cranial nerves and descends to the lower extremities in a presentation that may mimic SMA. However, this patient's weakness developed over the course of months rather than hours to days. Guillain-Barre syndrome (Choice B) results from the autoimmune attack of the spinal nerve roots and typically presents with acute-onset, symmetric, ascending muscle weakness with hyporeflexia. This patient's weakness instead progressed over months. Many patients also demonstrate autonomic dysfunction and/or sensory symptoms, which would be atypical in SMA. Myasthenia gravis (Choice C) is an autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission that may result in focal or generalized muscle weakness and fatigability. Myasthenia gravis demonstrates a bimodal age of onset in both young adults (teens to 20s) and older adults (50s to 60s). Myasthenia gravis in an infant would be atypical. Transverse myelitis (Choice E) is an acquired condition in which inflammation (eg, from an infection or autoimmune disease) affects one section of the spinal cord bilaterally, leading to acute motor, sensory, or autonomic dysfunction. This patient instead experienced the insidious onset of motor dysfunction only. Educational Objective: In spinal muscular atrophy, the bilateral lower brainstem motor nuclei and anterior horns degenerate, leading to progressive, symmetric muscular weakness and a lower motor neuron-pattern of dysfunction (eg, decreased tone, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, early-onset atrophy). Deficits typically progress during the course of months, which differentiates spinal muscular atrophy from the acute descending motor weakness of botulism.

questionStem: An asymptomatic 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . His parents both have essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia . He has an active lifestyle and plays several sports. He consumes a wide variety of foods , including meat, fruit, and vegetables , and drinks two to three glasses each of whole milk and fruit juice daily. He is currently at the 75th percentile for height and above the 97th percentile for weight and BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current weight?

choices.D: Inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables

correctExplanation: In children, overweight is defined as a BMI at or above the 85th percentile and below the 95th percentile for age and gender, while obesity is defined as a BMI at or above the 95th percentile. This obese child consumes a balanced diet but one that most likely contains excessive total calories. Common causes of childhood obesity include consuming a diet rich in unhealthy, calorie-rich foods, and a lack of sufficient exercise. Children from socioeconomically disadvantaged communities may face significant difficulties in obtaining healthy food and sufficient opportunity for exercise. Children with obesity are more likely to develop comorbidities such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Excessive intake of carbohydrates (Choice A) and excessive intake of fat (Choice B) are both correct but insufficient to explain this child's obesity. This child consumes a balanced diet as well as several glasses of both milk and fruit juice daily and is likely consuming an excess of both carbohydrates and fat, as well as protein. Inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables (Choice D) may lead to obesity indirectly by causing a child to consume an unhealthy diet that favors fatty or salty foods instead. This child does not have a history of consuming inadequate fruits or vegetables. Inadequate physical activity (Choice E) is a common cause of obesity in children. This child has an active lifestyle and his diet is a more likely cause of his obesity. Educational Objective: In children, overweight is defined as a BMI at or above the 85th percentile and below the 95th percentile for age and gender, while obesity is defined as a BMI at or above the 95th percentile. Common causes of childhood obesity include consuming an excessive amount of total calories, a diet rich in unhealthy, calorie-rich foods, and a lack of sufficient exercise.

questionStem: A 10-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 5-day history of a rash over the cheeks and diaper area that she constantly rubs. Her mother says that for the past 24 hours, she has been unwilling to stand . She is afebrile and otherwise healthy. Her mother and 6-year-old brother have asthma . Examination shows erythematous lichenified papules and plaques , and excoriations on the diaper area. She has red lichenified plaques on the cheek and chin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Atopic dermatitis, or eczema, is a chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disease common in children that is suggested by pruritus and recurrent eczematous rashes. The rash is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting and, with chronic scratching, becomes dry, scaly, and excoriated in a process called lichenification. Flexural dermatitis (eg, in the antecubital fossae) is a common pattern in children and adults with atopic dermatitis, but babies demonstrate a unique pattern, which primarily involves the bilateral cheeks and diaper area, as these areas are both frequently moist and subject to irritation. Treatment of atopic dermatitis begins with gentle skin care: minimizing long baths in warm water which causes drying of the skin, avoiding products with fragrance, and use of bland moisturizers such as petroleum jelly daily. In the case of an infant, keeping the cheeks dry and frequent diaper changes are also important. Flares of eczema are treated with mild- to moderate-potency topical corticosteroids, such as triamcinolone. In children, a moderate-potency topical corticosteroid should not be used consistently for over 2 to 3 weeks because of the potential of systemic absorption, particularly in the diaper area.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Candidiasis (Choice B) can affect mucous membranes or skin. Oral candidiasis demonstrates thick, white plaques on the tongue or buccal mucosa, which can be scraped off. Cutaneous candidiasis demonstrates red, macerated thin plaques with satellite papules. Candidiasis is a common cause of diaper rash, but in this case, given the additional findings on the face, atopic dermatitis is more likely. Food allergy (Choice C) rarely contributes to atopic dermatitis. Patients with diaper dermatitis caused or worsened by food allergy will also demonstrate gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhea, which is absent in this case. There is no role for specific food avoidance diets in the treatment of pediatric atopic dermatitis. Tinea corporis (Choice D) is caused by a superficial dermatophyte infection of the skin, most often Trichophyton tonsurans. The classic appearance is a round, annular patch with a scaly border. Potassium hydroxide preparation will disclose hyphae. Toxic epidermal necrolysis (Choice E) is a life-threatening adverse cutaneous drug reaction. Features such as skin pain, sloughing, or mucosal involvement are concerning for toxic epidermal necrolysis. This patient's lichenified papules and plaques are more consistent with atopic dermatitis. Educational Objective: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disease common in children that is suggested by pruritus and recurrent eczematous rashes. In infants, atopic dermatitis primarily involves the bilateral cheeks and diaper area, as these areas are both frequently moist and subject to irritation.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of the growth of pubic hair over the past 2 years . He is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb). He appears muscular . Pubic hair development is Tanner stage 5. Examination shows a mature penis. Testicular volume is normal for age. Which of the following is the most likely site of excessive hormonal production?
correctExplanation: Precocious puberty is defined as the onset of pubertal development and secondary sexual characteristics prior to 8 years of age in girls and 9 years of age in boys. Precocious puberty can be central, which is caused by activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. This early activation can be idiopathic or caused by central nervous system abnormalities, such as a brain tumor. Precocious puberty can also be peripheral, which is caused by the release of excess sex hormones from the gonads or adrenal glands, or potentially the ectopic production of human chorionic gonadotropin from a germ-cell tumor. Initial evaluation involves the measurement of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone {LH), and estradiol or testosterone, which allows the provider to differentiate between central and peripheral causes of precocious puberty. Central precocious puberty is further evaluated with brain imaging, whereas peripheral precocious puberty is further evaluated with ultrasonography of the testes, ovaries, or adrenal glands. Treatment is dependent on the underlying pathology. As testicular size is based on the production of FSH, this patient more likely has a peripheral cause of precocious puberty with hyperandrogenism leading to inhibition of the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), FSH, and LH. Adrenal causes of precocious puberty include congenital adrenal hyperplasia and androgen-secreting tumors. Treatment for precocious puberty is dependent on the underlying pathology.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Excess hormone production from the hypothalamus {Choice B) could cause central precocious puberty, which would present with increased concentrations of GnRH, FSH, and LH. Central precocious puberty can be idiopathic or caused by central nervous system lesions, such as an astrocytoma. However, increased concentrations of FSH in this patient would lead to a mature testicular size, rather than a testicular size congruent with the patient's age. The liver {Choice C) does not typically produce hormones. It does play a role in the metabolism of estrogen, thus a patient with liver cirrhosis can develop signs of hyperestrogenism, such as gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities, spider angiomata, and palmar erythema. However, liver failure is not a common cause of precocious puberty in children. Excess hormone production from the pituitary gland {Choice D) could lead to central precocious puberty with increased concentrations of FSH and LH. This can occur in the setting of a gonadotropin-secreting tumor, although these are exceedingly rare in children. As this patient has age-appropriate testicular size, peripheral precocious puberty is more likely. Excess hormone production from the testes {Choice E) can present with the peripheral precocious puberty seen in this patient. However, the most common cause of a testicular pathology leading to precocious puberty in young boys is a Leydig cell tumor, which would be expected to present with asymmetric enlargement of the testes, not seen in this patient. Educational Objective: Precocious puberty is the development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 years in girls and age 9 years in boys. It can be central, with increased FSH and LH concentrations, or peripheral, with decreased FSH and LH concentrations. Peripheral precocious puberty can be caused by abnormalities in the gonads or adrenal glands. In young boys, adrenal pathology typically causes precocious puberty with age-appropriate testicular size given the androgen-induced feedback inhibition of FSH and LH.

questionStem: A 3-week-old boy is brought to the physician 4 hours after the onset of vomiting watery, green material. His mother says that he has been drawing up his legs as if in pain while vomiting . He appears uncomfortable . He is afebrile . The abdomen is tender but not distended. An abdominal x-ray shows dilated loops of small bowel and air-fluid levels . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Volvulus occurs when a portion of the gastrointestinal tract twists, leading to bowel obstruction. Midgut volvulus usually occurs in children who have intestinal malrotation, a congenital anomaly in which the midgut incompletely rotates during development, and typically presents within the first year of life. The most common initial symptom in infants is vomiting, which becomes bilious as a result of the blockage of the small bowel and the retrograde flow of bile. In older children, abdominal pain is the most common presenting symptom. The diagnosis can be confirmed with imaging. Plain x-rays are acquired first to screen for perforation. Once perforation has been excluded, an upper gastrointestinal contrast series is obtained. Imaging studies may show evidence of malrotation with a small bowel obstruction including air-fluid levels and dilated loops of bowel. If not recognized quickly, volvulus can lead to vascular compromise with subsequent intestinal necrosis, perforation, and peritonitis.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Appendicitis {Choice A) typically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset, along with nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant on examination. It does not cause bowel obstruction or bilious vomiting. Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) {Choice B), also known as intestinal aganglionosis, is caused by the congenital absence of the distal portion of the myenteric plexus. This often leads to an inability to pass meconium within the first few days of life and may result in a large bowel obstruction. An explosive expulsion of feces on rectal examination is a classic clinical finding. Duodenal atresia {Choice C) is caused by failure of recanalization of the duodenal lumen. Duodenal atresia presents with vomiting and abdominal distension, as well as gaseous dilation of the stomach and duodenum on an abdominal x-ray. Foreign body ingestion {Choice D) may cause intestinal obstruction and bilious vomiting. However, it is more common in older infants and toddlers who tend to put items in their mouths, not 3-week-old newborns. In an infant, gastroesophageal reflux disease {Choice E) presents with frequent regurgitation without excessive irritability. Bilious vomiting is a warning sign of a structural cause of vomiting. Hepatitis {Choice F) can be caused by viral infections, autoimmune diseases, or medications. Hyperbilirubinemia with jaundice or icterus is often present. It is not a cause of small bowel obstruction or bilious vomiting. lntussusception {Choice G) occurs when an intestinal lead point causes the small or large intestine to telescope on itself. It presents with episodic, crampy abdominal pain accompanied by crying, vomiting, and bloody, mucoid stool. Pancreatitis {Choice H) presents with epigastric abdominal pain that radiates to the back, along with nausea and emesis. Acute pancreatitis can be complicated by necrosis, hemorrhage, abscess, or the formation of pseudocysts, but generally not a small bowel obstruction. Pyloric stenosis {Choice I) is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with non bloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings, and begins around 3 to 6 weeks of age. Educational Objective: Congenital malrotation of the intestines predisposes to midgut volvulus, which presents with signs of small bowel obstruction including bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. X-ray findings of small bowel obstruction include dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels.

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-month-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-day history of fever, lethargy, and vomiting. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 160/min, and respirations are 34/min. Examination shows nuchal rigidity and a bulging anterior fontanel. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL Leukocyte count 17,300/mm 3 Platelet count 262,000/mm 3 Serum Na + K+ Cl· HC0 3- Glucose 121 mEq/L 4.2 mEq/L 105 mEq/L 16 mEq/L 150 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's serum sodium concentration?

choices.C: Increased loss of chloride in the kidneys
choices.D: Increased secretion of ADH vaso ressin)

correctExplanation: Fever, lethargy, vomiting, altered mental status, nuchal rigidity, and a bulging anterior fontanel raise suspicion for meningitis. This patient's hyponatremia is likely caused by syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Release of ADH (vasopressin) by the posterior pituitary is typically stimulated by an increase in plasma osmolality but can also occur without stimulus in the setting of SIADH. SIADH can occur as an adverse effect of medications (eg, cyclophosphamide), a paraneoplastic process, or secondary to a central nervous system disorder (eg, stroke, hemorrhage, infection, trauma, or tumor). In this patient, the cause of SIADH is likely a result of meningitis. Treatment of hyponatremia involves treatment of any underlying disease and gradual sodium correction, typically with fluid restriction. A safe rate of sodium correction is generally no more than 6 to 12 mEq/day. When hyponatremia is corrected too rapidly, extracellular sodium exerts osmotic pressure that leads to the rapid efflux of water from neurons, which can lead to demyelination. The pons is particularly vulnerable to demyelinating injury and the rapid correction of hyponatremia can result in central pontine myelinolysis.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Excessive intake of free water (Choice A) can occur with psychogenic polydipsia, resulting in dilute urine and hyponatremia. It would be unlikely in this patient presenting with meningitis, and the cause of hyponatremia is more likely a result of SIADH. Factitious hyponatremia due to hyperglycemia (Choice B) can occur in patients with severe hyperglycemia. This patient's glucose is 150 mg/dL, which would not be enough to cause hyponatremia on laboratory evaluation. Severe hyperglycemia can lead to the osmotic shift of water from the intracellular to extracellular space, leading to dilutional hyponatremia in the serum. Increased loss of chloride in the kidneys (Choice C) would not explain this patient's hyponatremia. Chloride is typically reabsorbed with sodium in the nephron. The patient's hyponatremia is not caused by abnormalities of sodium or chloride reabsorption or excretion, but rather, increased free water reabsorption as a result of SIADH. The patient's chloride concentration is normal. Insufficient intake of sodium chloride (Choice E) would not itself cause hyponatremia as a result of the kidney's ability to reabsorb sodium and water to maintain a homeostatic serum osmolarity. SIADH impairs this ability by causing unregulated free water reabsorption.

questionStem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . Pregnancy was uncomplicated . He was born at term following forceps delivery for fetal heart rate decelerations . Apgar scores were 4 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . He is at the 50th percentile for length and 75th percentile for weight. He keeps his head turned to the right and cries when it is moved toward the left. Examination shows flattening of the right posterior part of the skull. A 1.5-cm mass is palpated in the left side of the neck. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient likely experienced an injury of the sternomastoid (also known as sternocleidomastoid, or SCM) muscle as a result of birth trauma, leading to congenital torticollis. Torticollis refers to an abnormal contraction of the neck muscles that results in the head tilting to one side. Congenital torticollis typically presents beginning at 2 to 4 weeks of age with a preferred head position, decreased cervical range of motion, and a mass of the SCM. Hypothesized causes include birth trauma (eg, forceps delivery) or intrauterine malposition of the head, which may lead to SCM injury and consequent fibrosis and contracture of the SCM. The fibrosis may present as a mass of the SCM on physical examination. Birth trauma or intrauterine head malposition may also lead to plagiocephaly (flattening of the head). The diagnosis of congenital torticollis is clinical. Treatment requires physical therapy interventions to stretch the SCM, which leads to the resolution of torticollis in most infants.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Cervical spine hemivertebrae (Choice A) refers to a rare condition of incomplete vertebral ossification in the cervical spine and may present with cervical scoliosis, neck pain, and torticollis. This condition is not associated with birth trauma and would not demonstrate plagiocephaly or a mass of the SCM. Craniosynostosis (Choice B) refers to the premature ossification (closure) of some cranial bone sutures, resulting in asymmetric skull growth in infants. Torticollis and a mass of the SCM would be atypical. Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (Choice C) refers to a heterogeneous group of conditions of neonatal central nervous system dysfunction that results from ischemic injury. Patients may present with decreased Apgar scores, an abnormal state of consciousness, a weak cry, poor tone, respiratory distress, feeding difficulties, absent primitive reflexes, or seizures. Similarly, prenatal stroke (Choice E) refers to a heterogeneous group of primarily idiopathic stroke syndromes that may present with nonspecific symptoms such as drowsiness, crying, poor feeding, and seizure. Focal deficits such as torticollis and plagiocephaly are more consistent with birth trauma, and a mass of the SCM would be atypical. Left or right clavicle fractures (Choices D and F) are the most common traumatic injuries during vaginal birth. Patients typically present with pain, swelling, and deformity along the affected clavicle. Syringobulbia (Choice H) refers to a rare condition involving a central cystic lesion of the brainstem. Patients typically present with lower cranial nerve and cerebellar signs along with involuntary movements such as torticollis and dystonia. Plagiocephaly and a mass of the SCM would be atypical. Educational Objective: Congenital torticollis typically presents in newborns with a preferred head position, decreased cervical range of motion, and a sternocleidomastoid muscle mass. Hypothesized causes include birth trauma (eg, forceps delivery) or intrauterine malposition of the head, which may lead to SCM injury and fibrosis. The fibrosis may present as a mass on physical examination.

During the past 2 weeks , she has had a decreased appetite , resulting in a 1 .4-kg (3-lb) weight loss. The family lives on a farm in Missouri , and the patient often plays in an abandoned chicken coop. Her direct contact to animals is limited to a pet dog and turtle. She has not travelled outside of the state during the past 9 months and has never been out of the USA. She appears alert. She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Histoplasmosis is an endemic mycosis secondary to infection with Histoplasma capsulatum. Pulmonary histoplasmosis can present in acute, subacute, or chronic phases, generally characterized by fevers, malaise, myalgia, cough, and hemoptysis with the associated development of small calcified nodules and mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Transmission occurs through inhalation of the organism's fungal spores. It is endemic to the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys in the United States, as well as parts of Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia. The virulence of Histoplasma capsulatum is dependent on its growth inside nonactivated macrophages, which protect the fungal cells from detection and elimination. Risk factors for histoplasmosis include exposure to bird or bat droppings. Diagnosis is typically made via the detection of histoplasma antigen in the serum and/or urine. Histology will disclose oval yeast cells within macrophages and caseating, or necrotizing, granulomas.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Both acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) (Choice A) and acute myelocytic leukemia (AML) (Choice B) are hematologic malignancies. ALL is more common in children than AML. The clinical presentations of both are similar, as they are caused by the relative burden of leukemic cells, including malaise, persistent fever, bleeding or bruising, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Neither would demonstrate necrotizing granulomas on lymph node biopsy. Chlamydia trachomatis infection (Choice C) can cause cervicitis, urethritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, neonatal pneumonia, and neonatal conjunctivitis. Other Chlamydia species, Chlamydophila pneumoniae and Chlamydophila psittaci, are causes of atypical pneumonia, which appear as diffuse, patchy alveolar and interstitial opacities on lung imaging. Q fever (Choice E) is a vector-borne illness caused by infection with Coxiella burnetii. Coxiella burnetii is acquired through the inhalation of spores from cattle or sheep amniotic fluid, to which this patient did not have exposure. Q fever commonly presents as pneumonia or endocarditis. Salmonella enteritidis infection (Choice F) causes nontyphoidal salmonellosis, a leading cause of food borne illness. It is contracted by the consumption of raw or undercooked poultry and eggs. Nausea, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea are classic features of salmonellosis. Tuberculosis (Choice G) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a slow-growing organism transmitted via respiratory droplets. It presents with primary, latent, and reactivation patterns. In primary disease, patients present with subacute fevers, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise. A PPD, or tuberculin, test identifies exposure to tuberculosis and was negative in this case. Educational Objective: Histoplasmosis is an endemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. It is endemic to the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys in the United States; exposure to bird or bat droppings are risk factors. Pulmonary histoplasmosis can present in acute, subacute, or chronic phases, generally characterized by fevers, malaise, myalgia, cough, and hemoptysis with the associated development of small calcified nodules and mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy.

questionStem: A 25-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 20 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She feels well, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated . Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation . She reports that her first child had bloody diarrhea as an infant when he was fed cow milk-based formula . The diarrhea resolved when the formula was changed to a hypoallergenic type . She states that she avoids dairy products because they upset her stomach . She asks how she can prevent food allergies in her next child. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation ?

choices.A: Delay the introduction of solid food until the age of 9 months
choices.B: Do not feed the infant eggs or peanut-based products until the age of 9 months
choices.C: Exclusively breast-feed for at least 6 months
choices.D: Use a hypoallergenic formula for at least 6 months
choices.E: Use a lactose-free formula exclusively for at least 9 months

correctExplanation: Food allergies are a component of the atopic triad, which consists of atopic dermatitis, asthma, and food or environmental allergies. Food allergies may be immunoglobulin E (lgE)-mediated (eg, urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis) or non-lgE-mediated (eg, food protein-induced proctitis, proctocolitis, enterocolitis). Exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is hypothesized to decrease the rate of food allergy in infants. Dietary avoidance of allergenic foods during pregnancy or lactation does not lead to decreased rates of food allergies in children. In actuality, introducing allergenic foods into the diet while lactating may lead to an increased likelihood of tolerance developing in the child and decreased rates of food allergy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Delaying the introduction of solid food (Choice A) or delaying introduction of allergenic foods including eggs and peanut-based products (Choice B) until the age of 9 months has not been shown to decrease rates of food allergy. In contrast, the early introduction of allergenic foods has been recommended in order to improve tolerance to these foods. Use of a hypoallergenic formula for at least 6 months (Choice D) or a lactose-free formula for at least 9 months (Choice E) is not necessary nor shown to decrease food allergy development. In contrast, exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is recommended. At 6 months, solid foods can begin to be introduced. Educational Objective: Exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is hypothesized to decrease the rate of food allergy in infants.

questionStem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of sweating and fatigue during feedings . His mother has also noticed that he seems to breathe fast and has a pounding heart rate at rest. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He is at the 50th percentile for length and 5th percentile for weight. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 145/min, respirations are 70/min , and blood pressure is 92/40 mm Hg. Examination shows prominence of the left precordium and a palpable parasternal lift. A blowing holosystolic murmur is heard best over the lower left sternal border. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: A left-to-right shunt from a large ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most likely explanation of this patient's cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, and failure to thrive. VSDs are among the most common congenital heart malformations. The genetic cause ofVSDs is heterogeneous and includes known associations with well-defined syndromes such as Down, DiGeorge, or Holt-Oram syndrome. It may also occur in isolation and via nonspecific, random mutations and individual point mutations that are de nova. VSDs are characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border and may have an associated palpable thrill. VSDs result in a left-to-right shunt, which increases pulmonary blood flow. This leads to remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature and resultant smooth muscle hypertrophy. In turn, concentric narrowing of the pulmonary arterioles occurs, which results in the development of pulmonary arterial hypertension. If severe and progressive enough, this can cause increased right ventricular pressures and associated myocardial hypertrophy, which subsequently results in reversal of the shunt (Eisenmenger syndrome), presenting with shortness of breath and cyanosis. Increased pulmonary blood flow results in increased blood return to the left atrium, which may cause left atrial enlargement.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Anomalous pulmonary blood return (Choice A) can be total or partial. Total anomalous pulmonary venous return is a congenital heart defect whereby oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins returns to the right atrium, not the left atrium. The presence of a second shunt is necessary to shunt blood from the right to left circulations. It does not present with a holosystolic murmur. Increased peripheral vascular resistance (Choice B), which is also known as systemic vascular resistance (Choice C), refers to increased tone within the peripheral vasculature. It is a normal response to decreased cardiac output in an attempt to maintain peripheral organ perfusion pressure. It does not explain this patient's presentation. Intermittent supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) (Choice D) refers to the presence of cardiac arrhythmias that present with a rapid heart rate originating from above the ventricles (eg, multifocal atrial tachycardia, atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia). ECG would likely demonstrate a narrow QRS complex with or without P waves. A holosystolic murmur is not seen in this condition and does not explain the patient's presentation. Educational Objective: VSDs are common cardiac malformations that result in a left-to-right intracardiac shunt. They may form in isolation or in conjunction with other malformations. The majority are asymptomatic and will self-resolve, but severe disease can result in pulmonary hypertension and the development of Eisenmenger syndrome, if untreated.

questionStem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of severe pain and swelling in her right sternoclavicular joint. Ten days ago, the patient had a sore throat. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . Her temperature is 40°C (104 °F). Examination shows erythema , swelling , and tenderness of the right sternoclavicular joint. Aspiration of the affected joint yields thick , yellow, purulent fluid . A Gram stain of the fluid shows numerous segmented neutrophils and numerous gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.D: CT scan of the left sternoclavicular joint

correctExplanation: This patient with monoarticular septic arthritis of the sternoclavicular joint from disseminated infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae should undergo arthrocentesis with culture of the aspirate fluid. Septic arthritis commonly occurs in children as a result of trauma to the joint permitting the translocation of cutaneous organisms (eg, Staphylococcus aureus) and may also occur in adolescents as a result of the dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted bacterium that initially causes cervicitis, urethritis, or pharyngitis and may hematogenously disseminate to cause septic arthritis. Septic arthritis classically presents with a painful, erythematous, swollen joint along with systemic signs and symptoms of illness such as fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia, and nausea. Gonococcal arthritis may present with monoarticular or asymmetric polyarticular disease and may feature adjacent tenosynovitis and dermatitis. The most common sites of gonococcal infection are the knee, ankle, wrist, and elbow, though the sternoclavicular joint may also be affected. In all causes of septic arthritis, serum laboratory values typically show leukocytosis along with increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein concentrations. Diagnosis requires arthrocentesis, which typically demonstrates purulent aspirate fluid with an increased concentration of neutrophil-predominant white blood cells. In gonococcal arthritis, culture of the aspirate fluid may disclose gram-negative diplococci. Management requires antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin along with source control.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chest x-ray (Choice B) may be used to detect late findings of underlying osteomyelitis (eg, erosions) in patients with septic arthritis caused by the translocation of cutaneous organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus. However, osteomyelitis is less likely to result from gonococcal arthritis. Echocardiography (Choice C) would be helpful in diagnosing gonococcal endocarditis, a rare complication of disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. However, this patient with symptoms localized to a joint most likely has gonococcal arthritis. CT scan of the left sternoclavicular joint (Choice D) may assist in the visualization of a joint effusion. This is especially true in difficult-to-examine joints such as the hip. However, joint aspiration is the preferred method for definitively diagnosing septic arthritis. Indium-labeled leukocyte scan (Choice E), a nuclear medicine procedure that adds a radioactive tag to white blood cells, assists in localizing sites of infection and inflammation, and is often used in patients with a fever of unknown origin. This patient possesses a clear source of infection. Educational Objective: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted bacterium that initially causes cervicitis, urethritis, or pharyngitis, and may hematogenously disseminate to cause septic arthritis. Gonococcal arthritis may present with monoarticular or asymmetric polyarticular erythema, edema, and tenderness. Diagnosis requires culture of the aspirate synovial fluid, which typically demonstrates gram-negative diplococci and an increased concentration of neutrophil-predominant white blood cells.

questionStem: A 5000-g (11-lb 1-oz) male infant is born at term to a 35-year-old woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Initial examination shows that he is large for gestational age and has macroglossia , visceromegaly , and an omphalocele . This infant most likely has which of the following associated conditions?
correctExplanation: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a genetic disorder involving mutations of any of several genes located at the 11p15.5 locus that may result from a variety of mechanisms, including defects of imprinting or uniparental disomy. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is characterized by cellular overgrowth and a predisposition to the development of malignancy. Its presentation is heterogenous but commonly includes an above average birth weight, macrosomia, macroglossia, visceromegaly, renal malformations, omphalocele, or umbilical hernia. Children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome are at an increased risk for developing a variety of malignancies, such as Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. Although the underlying mechanism is poorly understood, as many as half of children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome are affected by neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. The diagnosis is confirmed with cytogenetic testing.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Congenital heart disease (Choice A) may occur as either an isolated anomaly or in association with a variety of syndromes, such as trisomy 21. Congenital heart defects are not commonly associated with Beckwith­ Wiedemann syndrome. lmperforate anus (Choice C) may occur either as a sporadic defect or as part of syndromic associations such as VACTERL (an association of findings characterized by vertebral anomalies, anorectal malformations, cardiovascular anomalies, tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal atresia, renal anomalies, and limb defects). lmperforate anus is not commonly observed in association with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Polycythemia (Choice D) may occur in association with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, but it is rare in comparison with hypoglycemia. Neonatal polycythemia commonly occurs in post-term infants and in infants with mothers affected by gestational diabetes mellitus. Renal tubular acidosis (Choice E) is a family of disorders that causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and an inability to either absorb HCO 3-or excrete titratable acid in the form of NH4 •. Renal tubular acidosis is not commonly associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Educational Objective: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a heterogenous genetic disorder involving the 11p15.5 locus and is characterized by above average birth weight, macrosomia, macroglossia, visceromegaly, renal malformations, omphalocele, umbilical hernia, and an increased risk for malignancy such as Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. As many as half of children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome are affected by neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.

questionStem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of headache and dizziness for the past week . She has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections . At the age of 2 years , she received the diagnosis of vesicoureteral reflux and was treated with prophylactic amoxicillin until the age of 6 years . She has been admitted to the hospital twice for treatment of pyelonephritis . Development is appropriate for age , and her immunizations are up-to-date. Her height and weight are below the 5th percentile . Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 80/min , respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg in all four extremities . Funduscopic examination shows narrowing of the retinal arteries . Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Follow-up blood pressure measurement in 1 week
choices.C: Measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations

correctExplanation: Measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This patient with chronic vesicoureteral reflux and a history of recurrent pyelonephritis with new onset headache and dizziness in the setting of hypertension most likely has hypertensive urgency that has developed as a result of chronic kidney disease. Chronic vesicoureteral reflux predisposes patients to the development of recurrent pyelonephritis as urine from the bladder travels in a retrograde fashion to the kidneys. Recurrent pyelonephritis can lead to scarring of the renal parenchyma and loss of nephron mass, which decreases the glomerular filtration rate, and can lead to chronic kidney disease. Hypertension is a common complication of chronic renal disease and results primarily from impaired handling of sodium leading to expansion of the intravascular volume and subsequent systolic hypertension. Over time, chronic vascular remodeling and increased systemic vascular resistance lead to an increase in diastolic blood pressure. Assessment of the serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations is an appropriate first step in assessing kidney function. Increases in both are suggestive of kidney injury. Further assessment of urinary protein excretion is also appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Follow-up blood pressure measurement in 1 week (Choice A) is not appropriate at this time. The patient is presenting with symptoms, including headache and dizziness, that may be attributed to her hypertension. Further workup to determine the cause of her hypertension with simultaneous treatment is necessary. Blood cultures (Choice B) are not necessary. The patient is afebrile and has no flank pain or dysuria, making the diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis unlikely. Thyroid function tests (Choice D) are typically completed in the evaluation of secondary hypertension but would not be the first step. Hypothyroidism is more commonly associated with hypertension than hyperthyroidism, but patients also typically present with weight gain, constipation, fatigue, and cold intolerance. CT scan of the head (Choice E) should be considered in patients with focal neurologic deficits or severe, sudden onset headache, to rule out hemorrhagic stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage. This patient has had a headache for 1 week and has no neurologic deficits reported; a CT scan would likely provide little additional diagnostic information and would not be the best next step. Educational Objective: Chronic vesicoureteral reflux predisposes patients to recurrent pyelonephritis, which can result in scarring of the renal parenchyma and loss of nephron mass leading to chronic kidney disease. Impaired salt handling in chronic renal disease leads to expansion of the intravascular volume and subsequent hypertension. Laboratory evaluation should include the measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations.

questionStem: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of pallor. He has not had cough , rash, abdominal pain, vomiting , or diarrhea . He is alert but pale. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 150/min, respirations are 36/min , and blood pressure is 90/72 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities . The stool is maroon , and test for occult blood is positive . His hemoglobin concentration is 8 g/dl. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Meckel scan, or technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, is the modality used to confirm a Meckel diverticulum. This is a common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract and is characterized by a small diverticulum projecting from the terminal ileum that is approximately 2 inches in length and 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve. The diverticulum may contain ectopic gastric mucosa, which secretes gastric acid, leading to erosion of the intestinal mucosa and subsequent painless hematochezia or melena. In this case, the bleeding has caused iron deficiency anemia. Additionally, the diverticulum may act as a lead point for intussusception, obstruction, or volvulus. In a Meckel scan, the pertechnetate is taken up by the metabolically active gastric cells and visualized in the right lower quadrant, corresponding with ectopic gastric mucosa within the diverticulum.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. X-ray of the abdomen (Choice A) is not sensitive for Meckel diverticulum. It is the first step in identifying a small bowel obstruction or ruling out gastrointestinal perforation but will not provide information about the cause of this patient's gastrointestinal bleeding. Upper gastrointestinal series (Choice B) refers to a series of upper abdominal x-rays taken after the administration of oral contrast. This allows for the visualization of the proximal gastrointestinal tract to assess for a variety of conditions, such as duodenal atresia, malrotation, and midgut volvulus, among others. A gastrointestinal series is unable to identify a Meckel diverticulum. HIDA scan (Choice C) is a nuclear medicine scan used to diagnose cholecystitis when ultrasound is indeterminate. This patient's symptoms are more consistent with a gastrointestinal bleed secondary to a Meckel diverticulum than cholecystitis. Anoscopy (Choice E) refers to a direct visualization technique of the anus and distal rectum. Anoscopy is used to visualize bleeding hemorrhoids, which is another cause of bright red bleed per rectum but does not typically cause a decrease in hemoglobin. Educational Objective: Meckel scan, or technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, is the modality used to confirm a Meckel diverticulum. A Meckel diverticulum is a small diverticulum projecting from the terminal ileum, which may contain ectopic gastric mucosa and lead to painless gastrointestinal bleeding.

questionStem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of confusion , decreased awareness , headache , weakness , and dyspnea . When his mother returned home from work , she found him sitting in front of the television with the space heater on and an open package of cookies and glass of milk nearby. The most appropriate treatment is administration of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning occurs as a consequence of inhaling the gas, often because of its generation in an area of poor ventilation (eg, a garage with door shut and car running, a space heater in a poorly ventilated room, a malfunctioning basement furnace). CO is a byproduct of combustion. When inhaled, it avidly crosses the pulmonary capillary membrane and tightly binds hemoglobin, inducing a conformational change in the molecule and preventing the binding of oxygen. CO has an affinity for hemoglobin that is hundreds of times greater than that of oxygen, readily displacing oxygen from heme. CO also has affinity with the mitochondrial electron transport chain, thus, in addition to hypoxemia caused by interference with oxygen-carrying capacity, cells may not be able to make use of the oxygen they do receive via aerobic metabolism. As a result, anaerobic metabolism dominates, and lactic acidosis caused by hypoxia ensues. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, loss of consciousness, dizziness, vomiting, and fatigue; in severe cases, seizures, dysrhythmias, coma, and death may occur. Examination may show red skin. Treatment for CO poisoning begins with the administration of 100% oxygen regardless of pulse oximetry readings, and if any neurologic symptoms or signs of end-organ dysfunction are present, hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be indicated.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Acetylcysteine (Choice A) is the principal antidote for acetaminophen toxicity. Acetaminophen, in toxic doses, overwhelms phase II metabolic pathways (eg, sulfation, acetylation) with consequent depletion of glutathione stores; excess is metabolized to the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-P-benzoquinoneimine, a strong oxidant. Acetylcysteine regenerates hepatic glutathione stores, limiting oxidative damage. Amyl nitrite (Choice B) is an antidote for cyanide poisoning; nitrites induce the formation of methemoglobin, which in turn sequesters cyanide as cyanomethemoglobin, preventing its disruption of the electron transport chain. Its use is less frequent, as cobalamin also sequesters cyanide without interfering with hemoglobin and oxygen-carrying capacity. Atropine (Choice C) is an antidote for organophosphate poisoning and is a cholinergic antagonist. Organophosphate toxicity is common in the developing world; organophosphates bind to the active site of acetylcholinesterase, preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine. Resultant cholinergic excess leads to bronchospasm, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, diarrhea, lacrimation, and salivation. Atropine reverses the impact of cholinergic excess on the heart and lungs. Deferoxamine (Choice D) is an antidote for iron toxicity, which can be fatal in excess as a consequence of hepatic failure and profound metabolic acidosis. Dimercaprol (BAL) (Choice E) is an antidote commonly used to treat arsenic and mercury poisoning, though it additionally chelates lead and gold in serum. Methylene blue (Choice F) is an antidote for methemoglobinemia; it serves to decrease iron in methemoglobin to Fe2•, restoring its ability to bind and transport oxygen. Methemoglobinemia may occur secondary to the use of nitrites and anesthetics. Naloxone (Choice G) is an opioid receptor antagonist used in the treatment of opiate overdose, which presents with bradypnea and miosis. Naloxone has also been used to treat clonidine overdose.

questionStem: A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 4-month history of progressive fatigue and nervousness , intermittent blurred vision , and declining school performance . She has had a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight loss during this period despite an increased appetite . Her sister has hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine . The patient's temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Examination shows warm flushed skin and fine soft hair. There is mild exophthalmos and lid lag. Funduscopic examination and visual fields show no abnormalities . Examination of the neck shows an enlarged thyroid gland with a bruit. There is a fine tremor when her upper extremities are outstretched . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?

choices.B: Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland
choices.C: Malignant infiltration of the thyroid gland

correctExplanation: Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid condition caused by thyroid-stimulating autoantibodies that activate the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor. Hyperstimulation of the TSH receptor leads to overproduction of thyroid hormone and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland on physical examination, along with signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism including weight loss, insomnia, palpitations, heat intolerance, warm skin, tremor, diaphoresis, and pretibial myxedema. TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies also stimulate orbital fibroblasts and lead to thyroid ophthalmopathy, which is characterized by the expansion of orbital fat and connective tissue with resultant exophthalmos, lid lag, and restrictive strabismus. Thyroid ophthalmopathy may lead to diplopia, corneal exposure, compressive optic neuropathy, and a cosmetic appearance that is distressing for patients. Thyroid laboratory studies typically demonstrate primary hyperthyroidism with increased thyroxine and triiodothyronine, and decreased TSH. Radioactive iodine uptake nuclear scintigraphy typically demonstrates diffuse, abnormally increased uptake of the thyroid gland without a discrete nodule. Graves disease is treated with antithyroid drugs such as methimazole and propylthiouracil, and radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid gland. Thyroid ophthalmopathy typically responds well to topical lubrication, although severe cases may require intravenous corticosteroids and a staged surgical approach.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Levothyroxine overdose (Choice A) may present with signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism including tachycardia, hypertension, tremor, and anxiety. Severe cases may cause convulsions and coma. This patient's history of progressive symptoms over a four-month period, as well as her symptoms of exophthalmos and lid lag, are not consistent with an overdose event. Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland (Choice B) is characteristic of Hashimoto disease. While patients with Hashimoto disease may present with transient symptoms of hyperthyroidism during the acute stage, patients progress to develop signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism, including fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hyporeflexia, myxedema, and dry, cool skin. Hashimoto disease does not cause orbital findings of exophthalmos and lid lag. Malignant infiltration of the thyroid gland (Choice C) may lead to symptoms of hyperthyroidism through the destruction of thyroid follicular cells with resultant release of thyroid hormone, though patients are generally euthyroid. This mechanism would not cause orbital findings of exophthalmos and lid lag. Thyroid-stimulating hormone-producing pituitary tumor (Choice D) would lead to hyperthyroidism and laboratory findings of an increased serum concentration of TSH, as well as thyroid hormone. Educational Objective: Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid condition caused by thyroid-stimulating antibodies that activate the TSH receptor. Overproduction of thyroid hormone causes signs and symptoms of weight loss, insomnia, palpitations, heat intolerance, warm skin, tremor, diaphoresis, and pretibial myxedema. The presence of thyroid eye disease, characterized by exophthalmos, lid lag, and restrictive strabismus, is highly suggestive of Graves disease.

questionStem: A 2807-g (6-lb 3-oz) newborn has a strong cry immediately after delivery. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and a spontaneous vaginal delivery complicated by a few decelerations . The newborn was suctioned at the perineum and placed on the warmer/resuscitation table . After 10 seconds of warming , the newborn's pulse is greater than 100/min, and respirations are 20/min . Examination shows peripheral cyanosis and minimal movement of the upper and lower extremities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The initiation of breathing following delivery is crucial for the newborn. A substantial portion of neonates require assistance with the initiation of breathing. Initial, universal steps after delivery include an assessment of the newborn's heart and respiratory rates, muscle tone, reflexes, and color, and immediate warming, drying, and tactile stimulation, all of which are helpful for stimulating spontaneous respirations. Neonates who fail to respond to gentle tactile stimulation should be immediately supported with more invasive support techniques, such as bag and mask ventilation or endotracheal intubation. Tactile stimulation and oxygen therapy are noninvasive and are therefore an appropriate initial step.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Naloxone therapy (Choice B) may be useful for the immediate reversal of opioid toxicity in neonates. This neonate does not have any known risk factors for opioid toxicity and tactile stimulation is a more appropriate next step. Subcutaneous epinephrine therapy (Choice C) is useful for the treatment of anaphylaxis. This newborn has no exposure to agents likely to cause anaphylaxis, the most common of which is a food allergy. Epinephrine is appropriate for newborns with bradycardia in the setting of neonatal resuscitation. Positive-pressure ventilation via face mask (Choice D) and immediate intubation (Choice E) are both appropriate next steps if the newborn remains apneic and does not respond to initial efforts of tactile stimulation. However, these methods are both invasive and are not appropriate first steps. Educational Objective: Many neonates require assistance with the initiation of spontaneous respirations. Tactile stimulation and oxygen therapy are noninvasive and decreases neonatal morbidity and mortality.

questionStem: A 2-week-old female newborn is brought to the physician because of bruising on her arms and legs for 2 days . She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy . The delivery was precipitous , but the newborn fed well soon after birth . Examination shows petechiae over the face and trunk , scattered ecchymoses over the extremities , and an erythematous , fleshy irregular mass on the thigh . A bruit is heard over the hepatic area . Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 13 g/dL , leukocyte count of 5000/mm 3, and platelet count of 15,000/mm 3. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Large vascular neoplasms, or hemangiomas, including tufted angioma and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma, are associated with a consumptive coagulopathy characterized by severe thrombocytopenia and decrease in fibrinogen and other coagulation factors called Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. These neoplasms present as red or purple subcutaneous tumors. The increased blood flow may cause the affected area to be warm and swollen or even cause a limb length discrepancy. Signs of other hemangiomas, such as a bruit over the liver, may also be present. The large, convoluted vascular architecture causes platelet adhesion and trapping. This trapping leads to consumption offibrinogen and ongoing fibrinolysis, causing a consumptive coagulopathy. Patients present, as in this case, with mucocutaneous bleeding (bruising and petechiae), which could not be explained by trauma. They also demonstrate thrombocytopenia on laboratory evaluation. Treatment includes supportive measures to maintain hemostasis and treatment of the underlying vascular neoplasm.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Cutaneous lymphoma (Choice A) has a variety of presentations. It is rare in children, particularly in newborns. The most common type of cutaneous lymphoma is mycosis fungoides, an indolent cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Mycosis fungoides presents with scaly, wrinkled patches in sun-protected areas, more often in adults than children. Cystic hygroma (Choice B) and lymphangioma (Choice E) are both lymphatic malformations. Cystic hygroma may be seen in association with Turner syndrome as a subcutaneous mass of the neck. However, neither of these are associated with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome or the development of thrombocytopenia. Juvenile xanthogranuloma (Choice D) is an uncommon benign proliferation of histiocytes. It clinically appears as a solitary orange-pink papule on the face, neck, or trunk of a child. It is not a vascular neoplasm and does not cause Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. Mastocytoma (Choice F) is a benign proliferation of mast cells in the skin. The typical presentation is a single, orange-brown, leathery plaque, which forms a wheal upon scratching. Mastocytosis may also have presentations without cutaneous findings. Rapid mast cell degranulation may cause anaphylaxis but does not contribute to thrombocytopenia. Neurofibroma (Choice G) is characteristic of neurofibromatosis, a genetically inherited disorder characterized by a constellation of cutaneous manifestations including neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, cafe-au­ lait macules, and axillary freckling, none of which are present in this patient. Thrombocytopenia is not a typical clinical finding. Educational Objective: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is a consumptive coagulopathy in which a large, convoluted vascular neoplasm traps platelets and then activates fibrinogen and fibrinolysis. It is seen in association with tufted angioma and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma, both of which are hemangiomas that may be present at or shortly after birth.

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressive hair loss over the past 4 weeks . Examination shows a swollen and purulent area on the scalp. A photograph is shown . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp common in children. The most common presentation is scaly patches with alopecia. The patches of alopecia may demonstrate black dots that represent broken hairs. When a significant inflammatory response to the fungal infection occurs, a kerion develops. A kerion is a boggy and swollen lesion on examination. Tinea capitis is caused by dermatophytes including Trichophyton rubrum, Epidermophyton floccosum, and Microsporum canis. First-line treatment of tinea capitis is with an oral antifungal, usually griseofulvin or terbinafine. Close contacts of patients should be examined as the condition is contagious and can be spread through fomites, such as shared combs, pillows, or hats.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Topical corticosteroid therapy (Choice A) will worsen tinea capitis by inhibiting the inflammatory response necessary to eliminate the infection. Superficial dermatophyte infections treated with topical corticosteroids may become more severe. Tinea treated with topical corticosteroids is often referred to as tinea incognito, because of the severe and unusual morphologies that these infections take on after treatment with topical corticosteroids. Tinea capitis is a fungal infection, not a bacterial infection, and thus oral antibacterial therapy (Choice B) is unnecessary. Tinea capitis and kerion may become secondarily colonized with skin flora, such as S. aureus, in which case antibiotics may be necessary, but this is atypical. Oral antibacterial therapy is appropriate for bacterial skin infections including cellulitis, erysipelas, and severe folliculitis. Surgical excision (Choice D) is unnecessary as the infection can be treated with oral antifungals. In children, dermatologic surgical excision is generally reserved for neoplastic processes. No intervention necessary (Choice E) is not the standard of care for tinea capitis. Without appropriate antifungal treatment, the infection and inflammatory response will worsen. Inadequate treatment puts the patient's close contacts at risk for developing the infection as well. Educational Objective: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp common in children. When a significant inflammatory response to the fungal infection occurs, a kerion develops. First-line treatment of tinea capitis includes an oral antifungal, usually griseofulvin or terbinafine, along with the treatment of close contacts, if necessary.

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of increasingly severe abdominal pain. His parents say that he injured his stomach when he ran into the corner of a table 4 days ago . He cried immediately after the injury but then seemed to feel better. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Abdominal examination shows a 2 x 2-cm mass at the mid line. Serum studies show increased amylase and lipase activities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Children are more susceptible to intra-abdominal injuries after blunt abdominal trauma compared with adults because of less developed abdominal muscles, less anterior abdominal fat, flexible ribs that transmit force to intra-abdominal structures, and anterior positioning of the liver and spleen. This patient presents after blunt abdominal trauma with a midline mass, raising concern for a duodenal hematoma. Increased amylase and lipase concentrations have been shown to correlate with intra-abdominal injury after blunt trauma to the abdomen. Abdominal injuries in children may be subtle. Clinical suspicion for abdominal injuries should be raised when patients present with increasing abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent emesis, increased amylase concentrations, bowel obstruction, or sepsis. The initial imaging of choice to evaluate for a duodenal or pancreatic injury is a CT scan of the abdomen, which may demonstrate a duodenal hematoma, duodenal perforation, pancreatic laceration, bleeding, or other injury pattern. Duodenal hematomas can be complicated by proximal bowel obstruction as a result of the hematoma. Initial management may be nonoperative for smaller injuries or may require exploratory laparotomy for severe or persistent injuries.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. An x-ray of the abdomen (Choice A) may be used in the evaluation of severe bowel obstruction or perforation but would not be helpful in assessing for the presence of a duodenal hematoma. A barium enema (Choice B) is used to examine for abnormalities in the large intestine, such as colon cancer. It can also be used in children to evaluate for Hirschsprung disease and intestinal malrotation. It is not useful in the diagnosis of duodenal hematoma. A barium swallow (Choice C) is used in the evaluation of malrotation and midgut volvulus . It outlines small bowel anatomy and assesses the presence of an obstructive volvulus . Endoscopy (Choice E) is a procedure involving direct visualization of the upper gastrointestinal tract. It can be helpful in pediatrics for the evaluation of swallowed foreign bodies, gastrointestinal bleeding, dysphagia, or inflammatory bowel disease. Educational Objective: A duodenal hematoma can occur after blunt abdominal trauma in children. The initial imaging of choice to evaluate for a duodenal or pancreatic injury is a CT scan of the abdomen.

questionStem: A full-term 24-hour-old newborn has respiratory distress and seizures . Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . An x-ray of the chest shows diffuse hazy infiltrates bilaterally. Leukocyte count is 12,500/mm 3 (65% segmented neutrophils and 10% bands) . Examination of cerebrospinal fluid shows 4 leukocytes/mm 3 (90% lymphocytes) , a glucose concentration of 75 mg/dL , and a protein concentration of 25 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neonatal sepsis is categorized often on the basis of time from parturition, since the period of time in which symptoms begin may indicate which pathogen is likely involved, thereby guiding therapy. Early-onset neonatal sepsis (within 72 hours of birth) is marked by symptoms of lethargy, seizures, poor feeding, weak cry, and hypotonia. It presents with tachycardia, tachypnea, occasionally fever, and often with an examination that is nonfocal. If examination findings are present, they may reflect the source of infection or may reflect complications of sepsis such as neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Early-onset neonatal sepsis generally occurs as a result of pathogens acquired from the mother, either through hematogenous or transplacental spread or, commonly, contact acquisition in the birth canal. The most common pathogens associated with early-onset neonatal sepsis include Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), Escherichia coli, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and Listeria monocytogenes. Syndromes of serious bacterial infection include bacteremia, meningitis, and pneumonia. Late-onset neonatal sepsis (presenting 72 hours or more after birth) more commonly occurs from environmental pathogens in addition to those acquired from the mother. Pneumonia is more common in early-onset sepsis, and presents with cough, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, increased work of breathing, and rhonchi on auscultation. Workup for any suspected case of sepsis in a child younger than 30 days of age is broad, and should include a complete blood count, urinalysis, blood cultures, chest x-ray, and lumbar puncture at a minimum, since symptoms in this population are vague and nonspecific, limiting the utility of the history and physical examination to guide workup. X-rays in neonatal pneumonia disclose focal or diffuse airspace disease or may show diffuse interstitial infiltrates suggestive of respiratory distress syndrome. Treatment includes broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover the common pathogens.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Meconium aspiration (Choice B) occurs when the fetus inhales meconium into the lungs and is a known complication of labor and delivery. It presents with signs of respiratory distress (eg, cough, tachypnea, hypoxia, use of accessory muscles of respiration) and severity is a function of the volume of meconium aspirated. It is generally self-resolving when occurring in small amounts; large aspirations can lead to pneumonia or aspiration pneumonitis. Pneumococcal meningitis (Choice C) most commonly occurs in adults, whereas common pathogens causing meningitis in the neonate include Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), E. coli, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and L monocytogenes. Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carini1) pneumonia (Choice D) generally occurs in immunocompromised persons and was seen commonly in individuals with advanced HIV prior to the use of prophylactic antibiotics. Patients classically present with cough, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia, with rhonchi on lung auscultation and prominent perihilar and multifocal infiltrates on chest x-ray. It would be rare in a neonate. Respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia (Choice E) is one of the most common causes of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in children younger than 2 years of age. In the neonatal period, bacterial infection is more common and is also more consistent with bandemia and diffuse infiltrates on x-ray. Educational Objective: Common causes of early neonatal sepsis include Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), E. coli, and L monocytogenes, which are generally acquired during birth from the mother.

questionStem: An 18-month-old boy has had cough, coryza , vomiting , and diarrhea for 5 days and pallor and lethargy for 1 day. His mother states that his urine output has decreased , and the urine is now dark red. He responds poorly to stimuli. He has a grade 3/6 systolic murmur with a gallop and diffuse abdominal tenderness . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hematocrit Platelet count Serum Na+ Cl· K+ HCO3- Creatinine Urea nitrogen 24% 30,000/mm 3 138 mEq/L 118 mEq/L 6.5 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 2.6 mg/dL 60 mg/dL Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) is typically associated with infection from enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H? caused by the production of Shiga toxin. It classically presents in children with bloody diarrhea accompanied by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Other pathogenic precipitants include S. pneumoniae, Salmonella species, and Shigel/a species infections. This patient presents following several days of respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms, suggesting a bacterial or viral trigger. The abrupt change of pallor and lethargy, along with red urine and falling urine output suggests the presence of both anemia and renal failure. Physical examination may show petechiae, purpura, or ecchymosis, all of which are signs of thrombocytopenia. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates thrombocytopenia, increased creatinine and blood urea nitrogen concentrations, and often multiple electrolyte derangements depending on the extent of volume depletion and acute renal failure. Treatment is supportive and may include plasma exchange; many cases self-resolve. Generally, platelet transfusion is contraindicated because of the risk for worsening the degree of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia since platelet administration has been postulated to worsen the degree of thrombosis. If fever and neurologic symptoms are concomitantly present along with the anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is diagnosed.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Goodpasture syndrome (Choice A) is a type II (complement-mediated cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reaction that involves autoimmune deposition of lgG against the basement membrane in the lung and kidney. Patients present with hemoptysis and nephritic syndrome, which may be rapidly progressive and cause renal failure or death if not treated. Henoch-Schonlein nephritis (Choice C) is a vasculitis that classically presents in a child with renal failure and palpable purpura on the lower extremities following an upper respiratory infection. Patients often complain of arthralgias and abdominal pain, and intussusception is a known complication. Postinfectious glomerulonephritis (Choice D) is a nephritic syndrome presenting with gross or microscopic hematuria, peripheral or periorbital edema, and hypertension in a child, typically two weeks after infection with group A ~-hemolytic streptococci. Laboratory evaluation may show low serum C3 concentrations and positive anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers. Systemic vasculitis (Choice E) describes a broad class of diseases that encompass small, medium, and large arterial inflammation affecting various organ systems, commonly the kidney, gastrointestinal tract, and lung. While vasculitides may present following illness, the classic triad of anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure makes HUS a more likely diagnosis.

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . He is active and has been healthy except for an episode of otitis media 3 weeks ago treated with amoxicillin. His parents emigrated from Vietnam . His diet consists mainly of fruits and vegetables ; he occasionally eats fish and chicken but no red meat. Examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show : Hemoglobin Mean corpuscular volume Leukocyte count Platelet count Red cell distribution width 10 g/dL 64 µm 3 6100/mm 3 225,000/mm 3 10% (N=13%-15%) A blood smear is shown . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's anemia?
