correctExplanation: This asymptomatic child with mild anemia, microcytosis, and low red cell distribution width (RDW) who is of southeast Asian heritage most likely has either a- or ~-thalassemia minor. Thalassemia is characterized by the decreased synthesis of globin chains. Normal adult hemoglobin is known as HbA (a~2l and is composed of two a-globin chains and two ~-globin chains. There are four a-globin alleles and two ~-globin alleles. Mutations in one or two a-globin alleles or one ~-globin allele causes thalassemia minor. Thalassemia trait is common in southeast Asia and commonly presents with mild microcytic anemia. Supportive features include the presence of target cells on peripheral blood smear (pictured in the photomicrograph), a low RDW (which indicates that most erythrocytes are of the same size with little variation), and persistence of microcytosis. Iron concentrations can be measured to rule out iron deficiency. Other cell lines including platelets and white blood cells should be within normal ranges. Hemoglobin electrophoresis can be used to distinguish between a- and ~-thalassemia minor. There is no treatment required for thalassemia minor as the resultant anemia is usually not severe.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Antibiotic-induced autoimmune hemolysis (Choice A) can occur after exposure to penicillins and cephalosporins, but the onset is typically acute and occurs within hours to days. While hemolysis can occur weeks later, it is less common. Additionally, patients would be expected to present with normocytic anemia and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Haptoglobin concentrations can be measured and will be low, while the reticulocyte count will typically be increased. Iron deficiency (Choice C) is a common cause of anemia in menstruating women, strict vegans or vegetarians, and those with chronic gastrointestinal bleeding or celiac disease. It commonly presents with microcytosis, although often with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) that is higher than what is seen in thalassemia, and an increased RDW indicating the release of premature erythrocytes from the bone marrow. The measurement of serum iron and ferritin, which will be low, are used to make the diagnosis. Transient postinfectious bone marrow suppression (Choice D) may occur following viral infections, but more commonly presents with leukopenia, which is not present in this case. In patients with sickle cell disease, infection with parvovirus B19 can cause a transient aplastic crisis and severe anemia.

questionStem: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination prior to beginning college . She has had intermittent urinary frequency over the past 6 months without urgency or pain with urination . She feels otherwise well and has no history of serious illness . Menarche was at the age of 14 years . Menses occur every 3 to 4 months and last 3 to 8 days . Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. She is not sexually active . She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 80 kg (177 lb); BMI is 30 kg/m 2• Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a mild increase in hair growth over the upper lip and upper extremities . There are hyperpigmented , velvety, hyperkeratotic plaques on the neck, axillae , and groin. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Urinalysis shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) presents with irregular menses, infertility, hirsutism, and acne, often in patients with an increased body weight. It requires two of the following for diagnosis: oligo/anovulation, polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography, and clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (eg, hirsutism, acne). It is also associated with signs of insulin resistance, such as acanthosis nigricans and increased blood glucose concentrations, and is associated with an increased risk for the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Type 2 diabetes mellitus can be asymptomatic or present with polydipsia and polyuria, and acanthosis nigricans, as well as diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, if severe. Diagnosis requires a hemoglobin A 1c <?: 6.5% or a fasting glucose concentration greater than or equal to 126 mg/dl. Initial management includes weight loss and lifestyle modifications, with the addition of oral antihyperglycemics if these modifications are unsuccessful.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cushing syndrome (Choice A) presents with fatigue, hypertension, truncal obesity, hyperglycemia, fat redistribution, amenorrhea, and abdominal striae. It is a less likely cause of this patient's menstrual irregularities, polyuria, and acanthosis nigricans. Hypothyroidism (Choice B) presents with weight gain, fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, and menstrual irregularities. It does not cause acanthosis nigricans. Ovarian neoplasm (Choice C) classically presents indolently in an older, postmenopausal female with abdominal distention and weight loss. Some ovarian tumors (eg, germ cell tumors, choriocarcinomas, dysgerminomas) can lead to abnormal uterine bleeding. However, physical examination may demonstrate an adnexal mass, and symptoms of diabetes would be atypical. Urinary tract infection (Choice E) classically presents with dysuria, frequency, and urgency, as well as occasional hematuria. Physical examination may demonstrate suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis, in the setting of a urinary tract infection, will show positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, white blood cells, and pyuria. Educational Objective: PCOS presents with irregular menses, infertility, hirsutism, and acne, often in patients with an increased body weight. It is strongly associated with insulin resistance and the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus, which can present with polydipsia and polyuria.

questionStem: A ?-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of fever and cough. She was born at term following an uncomplicated delivery. She was treated for acute otitis media at 5 months of age. She takes no medications . Immunizations are up-to-date . She appears ill. She is at the 50th percentile for length and 25th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 80/min , and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 80%. Several 0.5- to 1.5-cm, mobile lymph nodes are palpated in the anterior cervical chain, axillae , and groin. Examination shows white plaques on the buccal mucosa . Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. The spleen tip is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 10,500/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 66% Lymphocytes 30% Monocytes 4% Bronchoalveolar lavage shows Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P carini1). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: HIV infection acquired via vertical transmission in the perinatal period is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with oral thrush, diffuse lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and Pneumocystis pneumonia. HIV transmission may occur at any time during gestation but is most commonly acquired at or around the time of delivery and in the immediate postpartum period when children are breastfeeding. Transmission is uncommon if the mother is taking antiretroviral therapy and has a low HIV viral load. As a result of universal screening for HIV in most developed countries, the incidence of perinatal and pediatric HIV has decreased, although this is not true around the world. Most patients present within the first few months of birth with recurrent pneumonia or opportunistic infections. AIDS-defining illnesses in children are numerous but include P jiroveci pneumonia, as in this patient. Initial evaluation should include measurement of the HIV viral load with concomitant testing for mutations. While this patient should receive treatment for her P jiroveci pneumonia and thrush, she should also be started on antiretroviral therapy once an HIV infection is confirmed.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Chediak-Higashi syndrome (Choice A) is caused by mutations in the lysosomal trafficking regulator gene (L YST) essential for normal formation and transportation of lysosomes within the cell. It presents with frequent bacterial infections, oculocutaneous albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and progressive neurologic dysfunction. Chronic granulomatous disease (Choice B) is caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency and results in impaired intracellular killing of pathogens. This presents as recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus with normal concentrations of leukocytes and immunoglobulins. Complement deficiency (Choice C), particularly of the terminal complement cascade, typically presents with recurrent infections with Neisseria species. Hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome (Choice E) is caused by mutations in the JAK-STAT signaling cascade, which impairs the development and function of T helper 17 cells (Th n). Patients present with recurrent skin infections, noninflamed abscesses (cold abscesses), and diffuse atopic dermatitis.

questionStem: A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents 1 day after she fainted during soccer practice . Her teammates said that she fell to the ground while running and appeared to be unconscious for approximately 15 seconds ; no abnormal movements were noted. There is no prior history of syncope , palpitations , or murmurs . Her parents are concerned because a maternal cousin died suddenly at the age of 22 years of an unknown cause . The patient is alert and oriented . Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.E: Admission to the hospital for observation

correctExplanation: An ECG should be obtained in this patient with unexplained exertional syncope. There are several high-risk cardiac conditions that can present with syncope in pediatric patients, and these can be classified as structural defects, including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, coronary artery anomalies, or valvular aortic stenosis, or can be a result of electrical abnormalities, such as long QT syndrome or Brugada syndrome. Evaluation with ECG is mandatory in all patients with unexplained syncope. Of these, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is one of the more common causes of syncope. It is generally inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and may be the cause of death in this patient's cousin. Syncope occurs as a result of left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction with a consequent decrease in cardiac output leading to decreased cerebral perfusion and syncope. Decreased perfusion of the coronary arteries can cause angina and increase the risk for ventricular arrhythmias, although this is not always seen. ECG classically demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy with non-specific T wave abnormalities in the precordial leads. Deep, narrow, symmetric Q waves may also be seen in the lateral and inferior leads. Echocardiography should be subsequently performed to evaluate the underlying cardiac anatomy, which would allow for assessment of the degree of LVOT obstruction, if present.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Reassurance (Choice A) is inappropriate. Patients with unexplained exertional syncope are at a high-risk for sudden cardiac death. ECG is a low-cost and noninvasive means of assessing for underlying cardiac defects and should be performed as soon as possible. Chest x-ray (Choice B) could be considered in patients with exertional shortness of breath, wheezing, or a prodrome suggestive of bacterial pneumonia, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with a cardiac cause of syncope. EEG (Choice D) is not necessary as this patient's syncopal episode was not associated with classic seizure-like activity. Often, seizures that result in syncope are preceded by an aura, and patients are typically confused upon waking, which is known as a postictal state. The patient's history is not consistent with a seizure. Convulsions can also be seen during syncope. Admission to the hospital for observation (Choice E) is not necessary. Had the patient not regained consciousness or required cardiopulmonary resuscitation, admission to the hospital would be appropriate. This patient should be advised not to participate in exercise until a complete evaluation has been undertaken, but this can be performed in the outpatient setting. Educational Objective: Exertional syncope is a characteristic feature of several high-risk cardiac conditions, including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. After patient stability is documented, the next step in evaluation should include ECG, which classically demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy and nonspecific T wave abnormalities. ECG can also help to diagnose conditions such as long QT syndrome or Brugada syndrome, which are other potential causes of cardiac syncope.

questionStem: A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by friends after they found her unresponsive at a party. There is no history of trauma . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min , respirations are 6/min , and blood pressure is 95/55 mm Hg. Physical examination shows constricted pupils . The abdomen is slightly distended , and bowel sounds are decreased . Neurologic examination shows a diminished gag reflex and generalized hypertonia . The most appropriate next step in management is administration of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Opioid receptors are G protein-coupled receptors located throughout the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS). Opioid intoxication causes euphoria, altered mental status, sedation, bradycardia and hypotension, depressed respiratory drive (or apnea), and constricted pupils. Miosis is a distinctive finding that is less common in intoxication with other CNS depressants and is caused by direct opioid receptor activity in brain areas responsible for pupillary control. Opioids also act on receptors within the enteric nervous system, decreasing gut motility and causing constipation. Opioid overdoses are characterized by respiratory depression presenting as a decreased respiratory rate, apnea, and hypoxia. Naloxone is a short-acting opioid receptor antagonist that reverses the respiratory depression caused by opioid overdose and should be administered emergently to patients presenting with respiratory depression in the setting of potential opioid overdose. Opioid overdoses can be complicated by apnea, hypoxia, and hypoxic-ischemic brain injury. Focus should be paid to the primary survey and management of the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation. This patient should also be transiently ventilated with noninvasive positive pressure ventilation such as a bag-valve mask while antidote is administered. Any failure of the patient to respond to the antidote or any further decompensation or airway compromise should result in emergent intubation and mechanical ventilation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Administration of activated charcoal (Choice A) would be unlikely to be beneficial in a patient with opioid overdose and would not be safe in a patient with altered mental status and a diminished gag reflex. Charcoal, if aspirated, can be harmful to the pulmonary parenchyma and cause aspiration pneumonitis. 5% glucose (Choice B) would be helpful for the treatment of hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia can also cause altered mental status and a decreased level of consciousness, but it would not cause miosis or respiratory depression as seen in opioid overdose. Methadone (Choice C) is a long-acting opioid agonist that is used in the long-term maintenance therapy of opioid dependence. It would not be helpful for the initial management of opioid overdose. 0.9% saline (Choice E) would be unlikely to be beneficial in this patient as it would not reverse opioid toxicity. Administration of 0.9% saline may be helpful as an adjunct for patients who may be dehydrated in the setting of substance use, but it would not be the initial step in management. Educational Objective: Opioid overdoses are characterized by miosis, altered mental status, and respiratory depression presenting as a decreased respiratory rate, apnea, and hypoxia. Naloxone is a short-acting opioid receptor antagonist that reverses the respiratory depression caused by opioid overdose and should be administered emergently to patients presenting with altered mental status and respiratory depression.

questionStem: A previously healthy 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 6-week history of right knee pain. She plays volleyball for her school , and the pain is worse after jumping or running . There is no history of trauma . She appears well. Examination shows a tender right knee; there is crepitance with flexion . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Patellofemoral instability is a common cause of anterior knee pain, which is caused by an anatomical defect leading to excessive movement of the patella. It is exacerbated by overuse and activities that put weight on a flexed knee, such as running and jumping. On examination, passive movement of the patella demonstrates increased sliding of the patella in either the lateral axis or superior-inferior axis. The patella may also be tender to palpation. The mainstay of treatment for patellar instability is activity modification and physical therapy. The goal of physical therapy is to strengthen the surrounding muscles and recruit stability of the patella from these muscles, as well as improve the position and balance of the limb overall. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may also be prescribed for use as needed.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Conversion disorder (Choice A), called functional neurologic disorder, involves neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. Though the symptoms disrupt daily life, patients with functional neurologic disorder may or may not be preoccupied with their symptoms. This patient's symptoms are not solely neurologic. Dermatomyositis (Choice B) is an autoimmune connective tissue disease that causes pink papules over the dorsal fingers (Gottron papules), pink to light purple patches over the upper eyelids (heliotrope sign), light pink to lilac colored patches with telangiectasias on the upper back and sun-exposed chest, dilated capillaries with dropout on the proximal nail folds, and proximal muscle weakness. Growing pains (Choice C) are recurrent, self-limited pains in the extremities that occur during childhood and early adolescence. Physical examination is normal. Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (Choice D), or systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, is characterized by fever, arthritis, an evanescent salmon-colored rash, and lymphadenopathy. Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (Choice E) is an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, which often presents in young males. The classic presentation includes a slow onset of hip pain that is worsened by activity and associated with a limp. The pain may or may not be relieved with rest. Neuroblastoma with bone marrow metastases (Choice F) is a malignancy of neuroendocrine cells associated with the sympathetic nervous tissue. Bone marrow metastases classically cause pain at night, and the patient would likely appear ill and cachectic. Septic arthritis (Choice H) results from a bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. The affected joint demonstrates pain, swelling, and erythema. Arthrocentesis is indicated for the evaluation of monoarticular erythema and swelling to evaluate for septic arthritis, which characteristically discloses purulent synovial fluid with >50,000 leukocytes/mm 3. Transient synovitis (Choice I) is a noninfectious arthropathy that presents with joint pain, often the hip, frequently following a viral infection in a child. It is unlikely in this adolescent athlete whose knee pain is chronic and related to activity.

questionStem: A 1-day-old, 1400-g (3-lb 2-oz) newborn has tachypnea , expiratory grunting, flaring of the alae nasi, and peripheral edema. He is cyanotic while breathing room air. Laboratory studies show: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: Which of the following is the most likely acid-base disorder?

choices.D: Respiratory acidosis complicated by renal failure

correctExplanation: Serum Na+ Cl· K+ HCO3- Urea nitrogen Urine pH Protein RBC WBC pH Pco2 Po2 138 mEq/L 100 mEq/L 4.2 mEq/L 14 mEq/L 12 mg/dL 6.2 1+ 0-1/hpf 0-1/hpf 7.17 50 mm Hg 40 mm Hg This patient's laboratory and arterial blood gas evaluation demonstrates a mixed respiratory and anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The metabolic acidosis is indicated by a pH less than 7.35 (acidemia) with decreased HCO3-. Anion gap ([Na•] - {[Cl·]+ [HCO 3·])) calculates unmeasured anions in serum that are contributing to acidity; in this case, the anion gap is increased to 24. Causes of anion gap metabolic acidosis include the ingestion of methanol, propylene glycol, salicylates {late phase), or ethylene glycol, along with uremia, diabetic ketoacidosis, isoniazid use, and lactic acidosis. In this case, a lactic acidosis secondary to inadequate perfusion of organs and forced anaerobic metabolism is likely the cause of the metabolic acidosis as a result of hypoxemia. If functioning correctly, the respiratory system compensates for the acidosis by increasing minute ventilation, which eliminates carbon dioxide, an acid. This results in a decreased pCO2 and an increased pH to approximately normal range. This patient's increased pCO2 suggests that respiratory compensation is not only inadequate but that there is also a concomitant respiratory acidosis. The Winters formula is used to determine the range of pCO2 if compensation is adequate: 1.5(HCO 3 ·) + 8 +/- 2. In this case, the range of pCO2o if adequately compensated, would be 27 to 31 mmHg. The measured pCO2 of 50 mmHg, outside this range, indicates an accumulation of pCO2 in addition to organic anions.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Both lactic acidosis with respiratory compensation {Choice A) and pure metabolic acidosis {Choice B) would demonstrate a metabolic acidosis with a measured pCO2 within the range predicted by the Winters formula. In this case, the measured pCO2 is well above that predicted range, thus respiratory compensation is not adequately occurring and CO2o an acid, is accumulating. Respiratory acidosis and metabolic compensation {Choice C) would present with acidemia, an increased pCO2o and an increased HCO3- concentration. In contrast, this patient has a decreased HCO3- concentration.

questionStem: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of pain in the right lower quadrant of her abdomen . She has had no loss of appetite . She was able to attend school today. Her last menstrual period was 24 days ago. She is not sexually active . Her temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 88/min , respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows no rebound tenderness . Pelvic examination is difficult to perform because of discomfort but shows a tender right adnexa . A pregnancy test is negative . Ultrasonography shows a 3.5-cm right ovarian cyst that appears to be filled with fluid . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The corpus luteum develops from the mature follicle after the egg has ovulated during the menstrual cycle. In some instances, the corpus luteum can form a cyst. Patients may be asymptomatic but can present with abdominal or pelvic pain if the cyst is large. Potential complications include cyst rupture or ovarian torsion. A ruptured corpus luteum cyst classically presents with unilateral pelvic or lower abdominal pain that is sudden in onset and severe, commonly after sexual intercourse or physical activity. In unruptured corpus luteum cysts, physical examination may demonstrate an adnexal mass and adnexal tenderness, as in this patient. A pelvic ultrasonography will disclose a cystic mass or free fluid in the pelvis if the cyst has ruptured, which may include hemorrhagic components {hemoperitoneum). Corpus luteum cysts are typically managed with observation and supportive therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous antibiotic therapy {Choice B) would be the appropriate treatment for a tuba-ovarian abscess, which presents with fever, abdominopelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, and an adnexal mass, commonly in the setting of a sexually transmitted infection. This patient is not sexually active, making a tuba-ovarian abscess unlikely. Diagnostic laparoscopy {Choice C) would be an appropriate step in the management of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, which commonly presents with vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain or peritonitis, a positive pregnancy test, and hemodynamic instability when severe. This patient's last menstrual period was 24 days ago, making an ectopic pregnancy less likely. Diagnostic laparoscopy would also be indicated for ovarian torsion or if the patient's cyst grew or caused persistent symptoms. Ovarian biopsy {Choice D) could be used to diagnose an adnexal mass. However, it is rarely used as it would lead to spilling of the contents of cystic structures and seeding of the tract of potentially malignant masses. Pathology for ovarian masses is more commonly dependent on excisional biopsies. Appendectomy {Choice E) would be appropriate in the setting of appendicitis. This commonly presents with periumbilical pain that later moves to the right lower quadrant of the abdomen, along with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Physical examination may demonstrate rebound tenderness, and ultrasonography or CT scanning is diagnostic. This patient's ultrasound did not disclose appendicitis. Educational Objective: A corpus luteum cyst may be asymptomatic or present with unilateral abdominopelvic pain if large. Complications include cyst rupture and ovarian torsion. Unless the cyst is suspicious for malignancy or causing persistent symptoms, observation, and supportive therapy is appropriate.

questionStem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a syncopal episode . At the time of the episode , she turned blue around the mouth while having a temper tantrum ; she then fell down and became unresponsive . Her extremities became rigid and shook and then became limp. After a few seconds , she resumed normal activity. She currently is alert, active , and well hydrated. Her temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min , and blood pressure is 94/52 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation . A grade 1 /6, systolic ejection murmur is heard at the lower left sternal border with no gallops or rubs. The cranial nerves are intact. Muscle tone is normal, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's syncopal episode?
correctExplanation: Syncope triggered by emotional distress in this 2-year-old girl was likely caused by a breath-holding episode. Breath-holding episodes are common paroxysmal events between the ages of 6 months to 6 years, typically triggered by stress-induced autonomic dysfunction. The typical sequence of events is crying, followed by breath-holding and cyanosis, then muscle rigidity and shaking, and finally limpness and loss of consciousness. Episodes may recur daily. Physicians should assess patients for iron deficiency anemia, which is commonly associated with breath-holding episodes, and treat with supplemental iron if deficient. Breath-holding episodes typically remit spontaneously.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Atonic seizures (Choice A) are generalized seizures that cause a sudden loss of muscle tone and consciousness. Complex partial seizures (Choice E) are focal seizures that feature focal motor or sensory symptoms and impaired consciousness. Stress-related triggers and cyanosis are more consistent with breath-holding episodes than seizures. In ambiguous cases, seizures should be ruled out using EEG. Patients with hypochondriasis (Choice C), commonly called illness anxiety disorder, typically present with persistent and excessive anxiety about the possibility of having or acquiring a serious illness. This 2-year-old patient does not likely understand the concept of a serious illness. Low cardiac output (Choice D) may lead to syncope but would be atypical of this otherwise healthy child with a physiologic flow murmur. In the case of frequent or prolonged breath-holding episodes, or a family history of sudden cardiac death, cardiac evaluation should be considered. However, this patient's episode was brief and featured a sequence of events typical for breath-holding episodes. Educational Objective: Breath-holding episodes are common paroxysmal events in infants and toddlers, typically arising from stress-induced autonomic dysfunction. Patients typically present with the sequence of breath-holding, acute cyanosis, muscle shaking, atonia, and loss of consciousness after crying. Stress-related triggers and cyanosis differentiate breath-holding episodes from seizures.

questionStem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 10 minutes after a firecracker accident ; he has pain and tearing of the right eye. The right eye appears normal. Both pupils are equally round and accommodate to light. His visual acuity is 20/20 . Ocular movements are full. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the eye pain?
correctExplanation: Loss of corneal epithelium describes the pathogenesis of a corneal abrasion, sustained in this example from debris scattered into the eye from a firecracker explosion. Corneal abrasions classically present with pain, conjunctival injection, tearing, and foreign body sensation. Visual acuity may be diminished, and blurry vision may be reported if the abrasion involves the visual axis. If the abrasion is large enough, it may be grossly visible as a discontinuity in the surface of the cornea, but if it cannot be clearly visualized, the use of fluorescein stain and blacklight or slit lamp may be required to detect the epithelial defect, which will be visible as an area of concentrated fluorescein stain, often in a linear or geometric pattern. Treatment includes irrigation to clear any residual debris, analgesia, and prophylactic ophthalmic antibiotic ointment to prevent superimposed infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Increased intraocular pressure (Choice A) describes a common finding in glaucoma. In children, this may be a result of congenital glaucoma, which presents with characteristic findings including buphthalmos (an enlarged eye), a large cornea, which may be edematous and opacified, and increased intraocular pressure. Infants typically present with epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm or eye rubbing. Inflammation of periorbital tissues (Choice B) describes the pathophysiology of periorbital cellulitis, which presents with erythema, pain, and induration of the eyelids or adjacent skin. The globe itself is not affected. Obstruction of the lacrimal duct (Choice D) presents with tearing (epiphora) from the ipsilateral eye, though it is generally not painful unless the obstructed lacrimal duct is also infected (eg, dacryocystitis). Retinal detachment (Choice E) can occur in the setting of ocular trauma; however, it is generally painless and is accompanied by visual symptoms of photopsia, floaters, and often with a visual field defect. Educational Objective: Corneal abrasions arise as a result of injury to the surface epithelium of the cornea and are diagnosed on gross examination or with the use of fluorescein and a blacklight. Treatment includes irrigation, analgesia, and topical antibiotics.

questionStem: A previously healthy 1-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of cough and difficulty breast-feeding . Her mother is concerned because the patient's face turns red when she coughs . She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy , labor, and delivery. She is otherwise healthy. Her mother has had a similar cough for 3 weeks . The patient appears thin. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F) , pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 45/min . Examination shows moist mucous membranes and clear rhinorrhea. During the examination , she has a long series of single coughs ending with a loud, high-pitched inhalation . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Episodes of severe paroxysmal coughing in the setting of a respiratory illness is concerning for pertussis. Pertussis occurs as a result of an infection from Bordetella pertussis and classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, which presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after 1 to 2 weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, at times violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, and pneumothorax. Often, such coughing fits are accompanied by cyanosis and may be followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The characteristic noise at the end of the cough is responsible for the colloquial name, whooping cough. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months. Symptoms resolve during the convalescent stage, which lasts from 1 to 4 weeks. Pertussis toxin is a major virulence factor that inactivates the G; subunits of G protein-coupled receptors in the respiratory epithelium and systemically, leading to uninhibited adenylyl cyclase activity and increased intracellular cAMP concentrations. In neutrophils and macrophages, this results in impaired recruitment, migration, and production of inflammatory mediators. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization in the form of acellular pertussis, typically administered along with tetanus and diphtheria vaccines (DTaP), but the first dose is not given until 2 months of age. This patient likely acquired the infection from her mother.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute bronchiolitis (Choice A) is often the result of infection with respiratory syncytial virus and is likely to present with fever, tachypnea, rhinorrhea, and wheezing. Patients may also display apneic episodes, but severe paroxysms of coughing would be atypical. Chlamydia! pneumonia (Choice B) is commonly preceded by neonatal conjunctivitis. It classically presents in infants with a staccato cough, in which each cough is separated by a brief inspiration. Physical examination may also show tachypnea and crackles. Foreign body aspiration (Choice C) symptoms depend on the size of the aspirated item and its location in the bronchial tree. It can present with respiratory distress and stridor, a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow through obstructed or narrowed upper airway structures, such as the pharynx, larynx, or trachea. Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (Choice E), also known as croup, typically presents with fever, rhinorrhea, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. It is commonly secondary to a viral infection from parainfluenza virus. Educational Objective: Pertussis occurs as a result of an infection from Bordetella pertussis and may lead to severe paroxysmal coughing, which may be accompanied by cyanosis and followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization, although this patient is too young to receive the immunization and likely acquired the infection from her mother.

questionStem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . She has no history of serious illness. Immunizations are up-to-date . Menarche has not occurred . She is not sexually active . Her mother asks if her daughter should receive the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine . She is reluctant to give permission to administer the vaccine if her daughter is not at risk for infection . The patient and her mother should be advised that which of the following is the most appropriate timing for the patient to receive the HPV vaccine?

choices.C: Immediately after she becomes sexually active
choices.D: At the time of her first Pap smea
choices.E: The vaccine is not indicated if she and her future sexual partners use condoms

correctExplanation: Because about 80% of people will be infected by HPV in their lifetime, the HPV vaccine should be administered to all patients. The vaccine should be administered at age 11 to 12 years, since the immune response is most robust before the teenage years and the onset of sexual activity may occur during the teenage years. HPV is sexually transmitted and is associated with genital warts along with premalignant and malignant lesions of the cervical, anogenital, and oropharyngeal regions. HPV vaccines have significantly decreased the incidence and prevalence of HPV and protect against HPV-related malignancies such as cervical and anal squamous cell carcinoma.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Menarche (Choice B) is unrelated to vaccine efficacy. The vaccine should be given to patients at age 11 to 12 years because of immune response patterns and the onset of sexual behavior, which are not associated with the timing of menarche. The vaccine should be administered to all patients regardless of risk factors such as sexual activity or condom use (Choices C and E) to promote herd immunity. Giving the vaccine after the onset of sexual activity would not protect patients from HPV infection, and condoms decrease but do not eliminate the risk for HPV transmission. The first Pap smear is recommended at age 21 years (Choice D). By age 21, many patients have initiated sexual activity and may already be infected with HPV. HPV infection typically occurs years before concerning cervical lesions may be detected by Pap smear. Educational Objective: HPV is a common sexually transmitted infection that increases the risk for cervical and anogenital cancer. Vaccination against HPV is recommended for all patients at age 11 to 12 years, since the immune response is most robust before the teenage years and the onset of sexual activity may occur during the teenage years.

questionStem: A 10-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of increasing fatigue and shortness of breath . He has had a persistent upper respiratory tract infection for 5 days that has been unresponsive to over-the-counter medications . His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1 °F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min , and blood pressure is 80/55 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and dry mucous membranes . Cardiac examination shows an active precordium ; a grade 3/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard along the left sternal border. His hematocrit is 16%. Which of the following is most likely to be increased in this patient?
correctExplanation: Cardiac output is most likely to be increased in this patient with severe anemia secondary to sickle cell disease (SCD). Adequate oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues occurs in several steps: oxygenation of the lung alveoli, binding of oxygen to hemoglobin in erythrocytes, and delivery of oxygenated erythrocytes to peripheral tissues with an adequate cardiac output. Peripheral oxygen delivery is mathematically defined by the product of the cardiac output and the arterial oxygen content. Arterial oxygen content is significantly lower in the setting of severe anemia, as in this patient, because there is a substantially lower hemoglobin content. As such, cardiac output must increase to accommodate a substantially lower arterial oxygen content if oxygen delivery to the peripheral tissues is to remain the same. This phenomenon accounts for the patient's active precordium and grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur. Additionally, this patient likely suffers from a component of sepsis given his persistent upper respiratory tract infection and fever, which would increase the patient's risk for concomitant septic shock. In the early stages of septic shock, the cardiac output is also increased in an attempt to maintain mean arterial pressure.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Central venous pressure (CVP) (Choice B) is likely to be decreased in this patient, who has evidence of dehydration including dry mucous membranes. CVP is often used as a surrogate for preload and correlates with the volume of the right atrium, provided the pulmonary artery pressure is normal. Peripheral tissue oxygenation (Choice C) will either remain the same or decrease further if the patient's cardiac output cannot maintain its increased state and/or the hemoglobin concentration further decreases. Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) (Choice D) is likely to be normal or low because of the patient's hypovolemia. In older patients with SCD, chronic high-output cardiac states can lead to pulmonary hypertension and increase the PVR. Systemic afterload (Choice E) is likely low or normal in this patient with components of both hypovolemic and septic shock. The patient presents with a severe anemia and evidence of hypovolemia on examination, which would typically result in an increased systemic vascular resistance in an attempt to maintain mean arterial pressure. This patient also presents with a persistent infection and fever, which may indicate a component of concomitant septic shock, which would result in a low systemic vascular resistance from cytokine-mediated arterial vasodilation. Educational Objective: Peripheral oxygen delivery is based on the arterial concentration of hemoglobin and the cardiac output. In states of severe anemia, where the hemoglobin concentration is low, cardiac output must increase in order to compensate, resulting in a high-output cardiac state, as seen in this patient.

questionStem: A previously healthy 8-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of fever, rash, and lethargy for 4 hours. She has had one previous episode of similar symptoms . Her brother died of fulminant meningococcemia 4 years ago. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 32/min , and blood pressure is 95/42 mm Hg. There are scattered purpuric lesions over the trunk and extremities . Her capillary refill time is 4 seconds . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: Complement system immunodeficiency is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with meningococcemia. Late component complement deficiency (CS to C9) is a common finding in patients who have recurrent infections with Neisseria species, and increases susceptibility to this pathogen through failure to form the membrane attack complex (MAC). Complement activation can occur through the classical, lectin, or alternative pathways, with each pathway converging at the point where C3 is cleaved by C3 convertase, releasing C3a and C3b. Following this, C3b is incorporated into the C3 convertase complex, which subsequently acts on CS convertase to lower the Km (increase the affinity) of CS convertase for its substrate, CS. Cleavage of CS results in the formation of C5a, a potent chemoattractant, and C5b. C5b complexes with C6, C7, CB, and C9 (terminal complement factors) to form the MAC, which allows for the creation of a transmembrane pore that interferes with the integrity of the cellular membrane, leading to cell lysis. Deficiencies of terminal complement factors impair the formation of the MAC and preferentially predispose patients to infection with Neisseria species. While most patients experience mild infection with atypical serotypes, they can also develop fulminant meningococcemia from typical Neisseria serotypes, as in this patient.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. AIDS (Choice A) can develop in pediatric patients who have acquired the infection vertically during the perinatal period from a mother with untreated HIV infection. Most patients present with evidence of recurrent pneumonia, infection with atypical organisms such as Mycobacterium avium, or with opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia. It commonly presents within months of birth but can also develop many years after birth. Child abuse (Choice B) should be suspected in cases where bruising is located in atypical locations such as the back or is with an atypical appearance, such as a linear mark on the upper arm. Purpura on the trunk and extremities is classic for meningococcemia and is far more likely in this patient with sepsis and a family history of meningococcemia. Congenital humoral system immunodeficiency (Choice D) is caused by numerous syndromes, including X-linked agammaglobulinemia, whereby B lymphocyte development is impaired by mutations in the BTK gene. Low or absent immunoglobulin secretion increases the risk for recurrent bacterial infections, but patients present within the first eighteen months of life. Increased susceptibility to Neisseria species, in particular, is not characteristic of this disease. Frequent exposure to multiple pathogens (Choice E) is incorrect. Healthy children are exposed to numerous pathogens on a daily basis and most do not develop invasive bacterial infections. While Neisseria meningitidis is associated with outbreaks in college dorms and military barracks, there is no such history in this case. Vitamin A deficiency (Choice F) is classically associated with xerophthalmia but does not cause the findings described in this patient. Educational Objective: Deficiency of the terminal complement proteins prevents the formation of the MAC, which is a critical component in the complement cascade, typically leading to the formation of a pore in the membrane of pathogenic organisms. Deficiency predisposes to recurrent and invasive infections with Neisseria species.

questionStem: A 4-month-old female infant is brought to the physician by her mother for a routine examination . The patient was born at 27 weeks' gestation to a 26-year-old multiparous woman after premature rupture of the membranes and premature labor. The patient's birth weight was 1200 g (2 lb 10 oz), and she spent the first 3 months of her life in the hospital. During hospitalization , she was treated for sepsis and respiratory distress syndrome that required intubation , mechanical ventilation , and umbilical artery catheterization . She is currently receiving oxygen and diuretic therapy at home. She is at the 5th percentile for length and weight. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 32/min , and blood pressure is 78/45 mm Hg. Breath sounds are decreased bilaterally, and wheezing is heard occasionally . Cardiac examination shows a pronounced S2 and a precordial heave. Abdominal examination shows hepatomegaly . An ECG shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these cardiac findings?
correctExplanation: Pulmonary hypertension is a potential complication of chronic pulmonary disease caused by the response of the pulmonary vasculature to inflammation, hypoxia, and pathologic remodeling. This infant has a history of respiratory distress syndrome requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation and continues to have decreased breath sounds and wheezing. This is consistent with a diagnosis of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, or neonatal chronic lung disease, which is a cause of pulmonary hypertension in infants. As the pulmonary circulation is usually a low-pressure system, the right ventricle is not equipped to pump against such increased pressures. Thus, pulmonary hypertension causes secondary right ventricular dysfunction, or car pulmonale. Car pulmonale is manifest by findings of right-axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy on ECG and chest x-ray with peripheral edema and hepatomegaly (signs of right-sided heart failure). The enlarged right ventricle is associated with a precordial heave on examination and a pronounced S:2, given the increased pressure of the pulmonary system impacting the closure dynamics of the pulmonic valve.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cardiomyopathy (Choice A) may be dilated, hypertrophic, or restrictive. While the right ventricle in this patient has hypertrophied, this is secondary to pulmonary hypertension rather than a primary disorder of the myocardium. lntracardiac left-to-right shunting (Choice B) is seen in some congenital cardiac defects such as an atrial septal defect or ventricular septal defect. Oxygenated blood from the left side of the heart passes to the right side of the heart, where it then returns to the pulmonary vasculature. If severe and untreated, the increased blood flow through the pulmonary vasculature can trigger pathologic remodeling of the vessel walls, leading to pulmonary hypertension. Right ventricular hypertrophy follows, causing a right-to-left shunt to occur. This phenomenon is called Eisenmenger syndrome. However, in this case, the pulmonary hypertension is secondary to bronchopulmonary dysplasia, not intracardiac left-to-right shunting. Peripheral pulmonary stenosis (Choice C) and pulmonary outlet obstruction (Choice E) are potential causes of pulmonary hypertension and increased right-sided heart pressure. In this case, the patient's history is more consistent with bronchopulmonary dysplasia as a cause of pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure. Educational Objective: Pulmonary hypertension may be secondary to bronchopulmonary dysplasia in neonates. Car pulmonale, or right heart dysfunction, may follow as a result of the inadequacy of the right ventricle to pump against the thickened, remodeled pulmonary vasculature.

questionStem: A previously healthy 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because of heavy vaginal bleeding for 5 weeks . Menarche was at the age of 12 years . Menses occur at irregular 30- to 45-day intervals . Examination shows no abnormalities except for blood at the cervical os. On day 21 of her menstrual cycle, her serum progesterone concentration is 0.5 ng/ml (follicular N<3; luteal N>3-5) . Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: The first half of the menstrual cycle, the follicular phase, begins with menses and varies in length. During menses, follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormone (FSH and LH, respectively) concentrations increase and stimulate the developing follicle. The follicle produces estrogen, which leads to the proliferation of the endometrium in preparation for the implantation of a fertilized ovum. As estrogen rises, a surge occurs, which in turn stimulates a surge in LH that causes ovulation. Immediately following ovulation, the luteal phase begins as the corpus luteum forms. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrial lining, which begins the secretory phase of the endometrium. However, if no implantation occurs, the corpus luteum degrades to the corpus albicans, and estrogen and progesterone concentrations decrease, causing menstruation and minor increases in FSH and LH. On day 21 of this patient's cycle, she would be expected to be in the luteal phase of her menstrual cycle, at which time the corpus luteum should be secreting progesterone. As this patient has a lower than normal progesterone concentration, it is unlikely that ovulation has occurred. Anovulatory cycles can lead to heavy menstrual periods, as estrogen is still being secreted by developing follicles to cause endometrial proliferation, but progesterone concentrations are too low to maintain the endometrium.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Gonadal dysgenesis 45,X (Turner syndrome) (Choice B) is a common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is a result of ovarian dysgenesis. Other signs include the absence of secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands/feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, fused kidney, and infertility. This patient has no physical signs to suggest Turner syndrome. Pituitary tumors (Choice C), such as prolactinomas, can cause menstrual irregularities. However, they are more commonly associated with amenorrhea than menorrhagia, and also may present with galactorrhea. A pituitary tumor would be a less common cause of heavy menstrual bleeding in this patient. Sexual abuse (Choice D) can present with abnormal vaginal bleeding caused by genital trauma, such as a cervical or vaginal laceration. This patient had no signs of trauma on physical examination, and trauma would be less likely to cause bleeding for 5 weeks. Von Willebrand disease (Choice E) is an autosomal dominant inherited bleeding disorder caused by a decreased or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor. It typically presents with epistaxis, ecchymoses, or menorrhagia. However, as it is an inherited disorder, it would have likely been apparent with prior menses, rather than occurring within the past 5 weeks only. Educational Objective: Anovulation can lead to abnormal and heavy uterine bleeding. A luteal phase progesterone concentration that is below the cutoff value is indicative of anovulation.

questionStem: A 9-year-old boy with chronic renal failure is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination 2 days after he began enalapril therapy for hypertension . He feels well. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a normal S1 and S2. No murmurs are heard. There is no peripheral edema. Serum studies show: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hyperkalemia?

choices.A: Acute progression of chronic renal failure

correctExplanation: Na• (mEq/L) K+ (mEq/L) Cl· (mEq/L) HCO3· (mEq/L) Urea nitrogen (mg/dl) Creatinine (mg/dl) Before Treatment After Treatment 141 136 4.5 5.4 102 100 18 17 55 57 3.1 3 .1 Enalapril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. ACE inhibitors are a first-line treatment for hypertension since they block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin 11, which has direct vasoconstrictive effects and promotes salt and water retention. Additionally, inhibition of angiotensin production has the secondary effect of suppressing aldosterone production. Aldosterone is responsible for the retention of sodium and excretion of potassium, and its suppression may lead to hyperkalemia. Other important potential side effects of ACE inhibitors include cough and angioedema.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acute progression of chronic renal failure {Choice A) would likely be accompanied by an increase in serum creatinine and evidence of fluid retention, such as worsening hypertension and peripheral edema. Decreased glomerular perfusion {Choice B) does not typically occur as a result of treatment with ACE inhibitors. ACE inhibition leads to dilation of efferent arterioles, which may produce a transient decrease in glomerular filtration rate but does not significantly decrease glomerular perfusion unless the patient has underlying renal artery stenosis. Metabolic acidosis {Choice C) is characterized by a decreased serum concentration of bicarbonate and is often accompanied by perturbations in potassium and chloride concentrations. Enalapril does not commonly cause metabolic acidosis. Causes of primary adrenal insufficiency {Choice D) such as Addison disease or congenital adrenal hyperplasia can produce hyperkalemia through the insufficient production of aldosterone. This patient's onset of symptoms shortly after the initiation of therapy with an ACE inhibitor is more suggestive of ACE inhibition as the cause of his hyperkalemia. Educational Objective: Inhibitors of angiotensin-converting enzyme are first-line agents for the treatment of hypertension and have the secondary effect of suppressing the production of aldosterone. Aldosterone is responsible for the retention of sodium and excretion of potassium, and its suppression may lead to hyperkalemia.

questionStem: A female newborn has mild cyanosis and a cardiac murmur 4 hours after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Heart sounds are heard best on the right. A chest x-ray shows dextrocardia with no evidence of pulmonary disease . Echocardiography shows a complex congenital heart defect with a regurgitant atrioventricular valve. Abdominal ultrasonography shows no evidence of a spleen. A blood smear shows Howell-Jolly bodies . This newborn is at greatest risk for which of the following?
correctExplanation: Sepsis as a consequence of asplenia is the most likely potential complication in this patient. Asplenia can occur as a result of congenital anomalies as in this case, trauma, or chronic thrombosis in conditions such as sickle cell disease. The spleen plays an important role in the clearance of bacteria, especially encapsulated pathogens such as Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Klebsiel/a pneumoniae, among others. It also removes cells infected with intracellular parasites such as Babesia microti. Thus, patients lacking a spleen are at risk for infection with parasites and encapsulated bacteria. The spleen functions to remove opsonized bacteria and cells infected with bacteria or parasites both by mechanical filtration in the sinusoids and through phagocytosis by splenic macrophages. Additionally, the spleen is a large lymphatic organ that houses many immunoglobulin-producing B lymphocytes. Any fever or sign of infection in a patient with asplenia should be treated immediately with antibiotics.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Anemia (Choice A) is not caused by asplenia. Erythrocyte progenitor cells exist in the bone marrow; therefore, erythrocyte production is not impaired in asplenic patients. However, the spleen does play a role in removing senescent erythrocytes from circulation. The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies, which represent erythrocytes with nuclear remnants, is typical of asplenia; these abnormal erythrocytes are removed by the spleen. Bleeding disorder (Choice B) would not be an expected complication of asplenia. Bleeding disorders can result from deficiencies in coagulation factors, von Willebrand factor, or platelet number or function. Cerebral infarction (Choice C) is not a consequence of asplenia. Patients with large arteriovenous malformations in the lungs, or large atrial septal defects, are at risk for paradoxical embolism with subsequent cerebral infarction. Thrombocytosis (Choice E) can occur following splenectomy, although this is typically associated with post-traumatic splenectomy. While platelet counts may be slightly higher than normal, this is unlikely to cause significant problems unless counts are over 1 x 106 cells/mm 3. Sepsis is a far more likely complication. Educational Objective: The spleen functions to remove opsonized pathogens, infected cells, and damaged erythrocytes. Additionally, it harbors a large population of antibody-producing B lymphocytes and thus functions in humoral immunity. Asplenia increases the risk for infections with both parasites and encapsulated bacteria. All patients should be given appropriate immunizations, including the pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus vaccines.

She has a 4-week history of temperatures to 40.6°C (105°F), facial rash, and diffuse joint pain. On admission , a diagnosis of hypertensive encephalopathy was made, and antihypertensive therapy was begun . Her current temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 45/min , and blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: An ECG is shown . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
